food.title: Food & growing
food.summary: How much land a population needs depends more on what it eats than on how it farms: land requirements per person differ by up to eight times between diets, and the average Swedish diet exceeds the global per-capita boundaries for climate, cropland and nutrients by two to four times. Urban growing gives high yields per square metre, but mainly vegetables and social value; the calories must come from the surrounding farmland, so self-sufficiency is a regional question rather than an urban one.

energy.title: Energy
energy.summary: The biofuel-fired Moskogen combined heat and power plant covers about 90 per cent of district heating demand and a third of the municipality's electricity demand, but solar power is highly seasonal and requires storage, flexibility and supplementary wind or biopower in winter. Offshore wind in the southern Baltic Sea has great potential, but in 2024 the Government rejected thirteen wind farms on defence grounds, which makes local generation, energy communities and energy efficiency all the more important. The costs of solar, onshore wind and batteries have fallen sharply since 2010, while Sweden's electricity demand is expected to more than double by 2045, creating competition for electricity, land and grid capacity.

mobility.title: Mobility & urban form
mobility.summary: Research shows clear health benefits of active travel (cycle commuting is linked to markedly lower mortality) and that urban environments with less car traffic, such as Barcelona's superblocks, can prevent hundreds of premature deaths per year in a large city. Experience from Pontevedra, Oslo and Ghent shows that car-free or low-car centres are possible, but the effects on retail and accessibility must be actively managed, especially for older people, people with disabilities and commuters from rural areas.

community.title: Community & cooperation
community.summary: Social relationships are as strong a survival factor as well-known risk factors: meta-analyses show a 50% higher likelihood of survival for people with strong social ties, and the WHO links loneliness to about 871,000 deaths a year worldwide. The municipality can influence this through social infrastructure (libraries, meeting places, green spaces, activities in residential care homes), community and intergenerational housing, deliberative democracy (citizens' assemblies, participatory budgeting) and working-time trials that free up time for relationships and civic engagement. The evidence is strong for the link between loneliness and health but weaker and more context-dependent for the effect of individual measures, which the model should reflect with cautious effect sizes.

health.title: Health
health.summary: Strong evidence shows that nature and greenery close to home (at least 120 minutes in nature a week, a green space within 300 metres) and physical activity (150–300 minutes a week) prevent both physical and mental ill-health, and that preventive public health measures on average return several kronor for every krona invested. At the same time, psychosomatic complaints among young people are rising – 77% of 15-year-old girls have recurring complaints – and only one in five schoolchildren is sufficiently active.

digital_resilience.title: De-digitalisation & digital resilience
digital_resilience.summary: Since 2023, Sweden has swung from “digital first” in schools to analogue teaching materials, a phone-free school day (law from 1 August 2026) and national screen-time recommendations for children. At the same time, the state is building up analogue back-up capacity in the payment system: legal requirements that grocery stores and pharmacies accept cash and offline card payments for essential goods for up to seven days apply from 1 July 2026. The evidence on screen and phone restrictions is mixed – some studies show improved results for low-performing pupils and girls, others no effect on well-being. A coastal municipality with many older residents and a location close to the security-policy tensions around the Baltic Sea has particular reasons to plan for outages in electricity, telecoms and payments.

tech_ai.title: Acceleration with technology & AI
tech_ai.summary: The evidence points to a few areas where AI delivers large, documented public benefit: a Swedish randomised trial (MASAI) shows that AI-supported mammography finds 29% more cancers with a 44% lower reading workload, AI can shorten power outages by 30–50% and give flood warnings several days earlier, and AI-supported interpreting can sharply reduce costs in the public sector. At the same time there are clear risks: data centres’ electricity demand is expected to more than double by 2030, professional skills can erode (endoscopists detected fewer polyps after getting used to AI), and surveillance is restricted only by the EU AI Act. The AI Commission’s roadmap (SOU 2025:12) proposes 75 measures costing just under SEK 17 billion over ten years and notes that many smaller municipalities have not even begun using AI.

resilience.title: Preparedness & resilience
resilience.summary: Sweden’s total defence planning assumes that society must be able to cope with at least three months of a security policy crisis, including war, and households are urged by the Swedish Civil Defence and Resilience Agency (MCF, formerly the Swedish Civil Contingencies Agency, MSB) to manage on their own for at least one week. The security situation in the Baltic Sea has become more tense since Sweden joined NATO in 2024 and since several undersea cables and gas pipelines were damaged in 2023–2024. Preparedness in the game is therefore about both war/crisis (days of self-sufficiency) and slow-onset climate risks (water, sea level).

biodiversity_baltic.title: Biodiversity & the Baltic Sea
biodiversity_baltic.summary: Over 96% of the Baltic Sea is not in good status with regard to eutrophication, oxygen-free seabeds have increased tenfold in a century, the eastern Baltic cod stock has collapsed, and along the Swedish coast the three-spined stickleback has taken over from perch and pike in more and more bays. There are proven measures with known effects: wetlands, catch crops, better wastewater treatment and protected areas, but the Baltic Sea responds with a delay of decades.

governance.title: Long-term governance & vision
governance.summary: Long-term governance is about giving future generations a voice in today’s decisions. The Welsh Well-being of Future Generations Act (2015) and Finland’s Committee for the Future (since 1993) show that long-term thinking can be institutionalised, but evaluations show that the effect depends on whether it is tied to budgets and investment. The Doughnut model (Raworth 2017) and the Stockholm Resilience Centre’s “wedding cake” provide frameworks for a good life within planetary boundaries, and Amsterdam and Tomelilla already use them in their governance. In the game, the player can build the institutions for responsibility towards the future that are missing today.

demography.title: Demography 2026–2126
demography.summary: Sweden is growing slowly and ageing: the Statistics Sweden (SCB) projection gives 11.8 million inhabitants in 2070 and – in the statistical database’s extension – just under 13 million in 2120, driven almost entirely by immigration because more people die than are born. Fertility is at a record low (1.43 children per woman in 2024 and 2025), and the share of people aged 80 and over is expected to almost double by 2070. Swedes unusually often live alone and leave home early, so multigenerational living would be a real cultural change. There are no official municipal projections beyond 2070 – the game’s values for 2070–2126 are explicit assumptions.

food_e1.claim: The average American diet requires about 1.08 hectares of agricultural land per person per year – the most of ten diet scenarios studied.
food_e1.context: Biophysical model of US agricultural land (cropland + pasture) with ten diet scenarios; land requirements ranged from 0.13 to 1.08 ha/person/year and carrying capacity from 402 to 807 million people. Used as an upper reference point for a meat-heavy Western diet.

food_e2.claim: The plant-based (vegan) diet required the least land (about 0.13 ha/person/year, roughly one eighth of the baseline diet), but the lacto-vegetarian diet gave the highest carrying capacity, and the vegan diet a lower carrying capacity than two healthy mixed diets.
food_e2.context: The paradox is explained by the fact that pasture that cannot be used for crops is only useful via ruminants. The one-eighth figure is from Tufts' press release.

food_e3.claim: A global shift to a plant-based diet would reduce agricultural land by about 76% (about 3.1 billion hectares).
food_e3.context: Meta-analysis of life-cycle data from about 38,700 farms and 1,600 processors/retailers. Impacts vary up to 50-fold between producers of the same product, but even the lowest-impact animal products usually have higher impacts than plant-based alternatives. The 76% figure has been verified via secondary summaries (press material), not directly in the article text; hence medium confidence. Used as an upper limit for land savings from a dietary shift.

food_e4.claim: 'Fair' Swedish diets that use no more arable land than the globally available amount per capita, and in which animals are raised on pasture and by-products ('ecological leftovers'), have a considerably lower environmental impact than today's Swedish diet – but still exceed the climate boundary and the nitrogen/phosphorus boundaries.
food_e4.context: Scenario analysis for Sweden in which semi-natural pastures are grazed by ruminants for biodiversity reasons; the scenarios gave, for example, 0–350 ml of milk per day and meat two to four times a week. Qualitative basis for the 'animals on pasture and leftovers' principle in the model.

food_e5.claim: A Nordic organic food system with no competition between food and feed could feed 109–130% of the projected Nordic population in 2030, but with 81% less meat than today.
food_e5.context: Modelling study (SLU, Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences) in which animals eat only pasture, ley from the crop rotation and by-products, and in which agriculture is self-sufficient in bioenergy. Shows that lower organic yields can be offset by a dietary shift. Trade-off: more ley for animals gives more food overall but a larger climate impact per person. Nitrogen and phosphorus deficits require increased recycling of nutrients from society.

food_e6.claim: The average Swedish diet exceeds the global EAT-Lancet boundaries (converted per capita) for greenhouse gases, cropland and nutrient inputs by two to more than four times, and for biodiversity by six times.
food_e6.context: Benchmarking of the Swedish diet (SLU/SEI, Stockholm Environment Institute). Freshwater use was within the boundary. Can be used as the starting value for the indicator 'the diet's pressure on planetary boundaries' in 2026 (value ~2–4 for climate/land/N-P, 6 for biodiversity).

food_e7.claim: Total consumption of red meat (beef, mutton/lamb, pork) in Sweden was about 53 kg per person in 2025 (preliminary, bone-in weight); all meat including poultry about 80 kg.
food_e7.context: Swedish Board of Agriculture consumption statistics 2025, preliminary: beef 22.41, mutton 1.61, pork 29.30, poultry 23.36, total meat 79.92 kg/person. Corresponds to about 146 g of red meat per day calculated bone-in; the edible amount is lower, but even after conversion the intake is several times above the EAT-Lancet reference of 15 g/day (food_e9). Starting value for the diet indicator.

food_e8.claim: In 2024 Swedes consumed about 65.5 kg of fresh and frozen vegetables and 53.7 kg of fresh and frozen fruit and berries per person.
food_e8.context: Swedish Board of Agriculture total consumption 2024 (preliminary). Processed vegetables/fruit come on top of this.

food_e9.claim: The EAT-Lancet Commission's planetary health diet (2025) specifies about 15 g of red meat per day (range 0–30 g) within an average energy intake of about 2,400 kcal/day; half the plate fruit and vegetables (300 g vegetables, 200 g fruit), 75 g legumes, 50 g nuts, 210 g whole grains.
food_e9.context: Updated reference diet from EAT-Lancet 2.0 (Rockström, Thilsted, Willett et al. 2025). Other reference amounts: dairy 250 g (0–500), poultry 30 g (0–60), fish 30 g (0–100), eggs 15 g (0–25). Used as the target diet ('planetary health diet') in the game's diet indicator.

food_e10.claim: If the world ate according to the planetary health diet, about 15 million premature deaths per year could be avoided, around 27% of global mortality.
food_e10.context: Model calculation in EAT-Lancet 2025. The largest effect comes when dietary change, reduced food waste and more efficient/sustainable production are combined. Can be translated into the health indicator as a relative reduction in the diet-related disease burden; Sweden's share is lower than the global one because undernutrition is absent.

food_e11.claim: Food systems account for nearly 30% of global greenhouse gas emissions and for almost the entire overshoot of the nitrogen and phosphorus boundary; only about 1% of the world's population lives within a 'safe and just' space.
food_e11.context: EAT-Lancet 2025. According to the Commission, food-related emissions should come down to about 5 Gt CO2e/year by 2050; agriculture has already converted 37% of the Earth's ice-free land area. Links directly to the ecological ceiling of the Doughnut model (climate, land, nitrogen/phosphorus).

food_e12.claim: In 2025 Sweden had about 2.53 million hectares of arable land, corresponding to roughly 0.24 hectares per inhabitant.
food_e12.context: Own calculation: 2,526,869 ha of arable land in 2025 (Swedish Board of Agriculture, JO0104B1) divided by 10,605,529 inhabitants on 31 Dec 2025 (Statistics Sweden (SCB)). Arable land has decreased slightly (2,529,820 ha in 2023). Of which cereals about 1.01 million ha and ley about 1.06 million ha.

food_e16.claim: Roughly every second mouthful eaten in Sweden is produced in the country (a self-sufficiency rate of around 50%).
food_e16.context: LRF's (the Federation of Swedish Farmers') wording on its preparedness page. LRF proposes emergency stockpiles of grain and farm inputs (fertiliser, feed, fuel). The Swedish Board of Agriculture explicitly does not calculate an overall self-sufficiency rate. Instead, the agency reports 'supply capacity' per product group (see food_e46) and points out that production depends on imported inputs. The figure is therefore a rough benchmark used in politics, not an official measure. Use 50% as a rough national starting value.

food_e17.claim: The state has resumed emergency stockpiling of food: the Swedish Food Agency stores freeze-dried food in the four northernmost counties via framework agreements with five companies and proposes that the state purchase mobile mills; public kitchens are urged to plan crisis menus and stocks.
food_e17.context: The Swedish Food Agency's pages on emergency stockpiling and crisis preparedness for public kitchens (reviewed 2026-05-05). Investment support is available through the preparedness sector's investment programme, but there are no national requirements on the number of days for municipal kitchens – the municipality decides for itself. Basis for the game's preparedness lever.

food_e18.claim: With the global potential of near-urban (peri-urban) agriculture, about 1 billion city dwellers, around 30% of the world's urban population, could be supplied locally; the share falls to about 22% by 2050 and is about 20% in North America.
food_e18.context: Global model (PIK) using remote sensing, population and climate data; 35% with optimised yields. Urbanisation is the biggest pressure factor, followed by dietary changes and climate. Optimised local supply could reduce transport emissions tenfold (but transport is a small part of food's climate impact).

food_e19.claim: Current home growing in gardens and allotments in a British town (Bedford) is enough to supply residents' fruit and vegetables for about 30 days a year; in the most optimistic scenario, land already under cultivation could cover over half of annual needs.
food_e19.context: Combines yield data from home growers with mapping of gardens, allotments and fruit trees. Corresponds to about 8% of fruit and vegetable needs today and up to 50% with a major scale-up on existing land. Fruit/vegetables only, not calories.

food_e20.claim: Allotments on 1.5% of Leicester's urban area provide fruit and vegetables for about 3% of the population (over 1,200 tonnes of fruit/vegetables and 200 tonnes of potatoes per year); yields per unit area were similar to commercial horticulture.
food_e20.context: Citizen science + GIS. Only about 52% of the allotment area was used for growing. In the 1950s there were 475 ha of allotments (compared with 97 ha today), which supplied over 45,000 people. Shows the potential of restoring allotment areas. Figures verified via a summary of the article.

food_e21.claim: Small-scale organic urban farms in Sydney yielded on average 5.94 kg of vegetables per m² per year – roughly double the yield on commercial vegetable farms (3.18 kg/m²) – but labour productivity was only 1.29 kg per working hour.
food_e21.context: 13 farms followed for one year. Benefit/cost ratio 0.62 when working time is valued (2.81 without labour costs); only 14.7% of inputs were renewable (purchased compost, municipal water). Upper realistic value for intensive small-scale growing; very labour-intensive – better suited as a leisure/social activity than commercial production.

food_e22.claim: Urban growers in Brighton and Hove harvested around 1 kg of insect-pollinated fruit and vegetables per m² per season, comparable to conventional farms, and recorded over 2,000 pollinating insects in their plots.
food_e22.context: Case study in a review of urban agriculture's contribution to the Global Goals. The figure applies only to insect-pollinated crops and is taken from press material about the study; the article stresses large knowledge gaps about productivity and economics. A reasonably low value for allotments in a temperate climate.

food_e23.claim: Global meta-analysis (200 studies, 2,062 observations): urban agriculture yields are on a par with or higher than conventional agriculture; the largest difference was for cucumber (17 kg/m² per growing cycle versus 3.8 kg/m²).
food_e23.context: Yields per growing cycle – several cycles per year are possible in greenhouses/indoors, fewer outdoors in Sweden. Hydroponic tomatoes gave significantly higher yields than soil-grown ones. Lettuce/chicory were the most commonly studied. Use for relative comparison between growing systems.

food_e24.claim: In 2025 Swedish commercial greenhouses harvested on average about 36.5 kg of tomatoes and 50 kg of cucumbers per m² of greenhouse area.
food_e24.context: Own calculation from Swedish Board of Agriculture data: tomatoes 17,700 tonnes on 484,500 m², cucumbers 31,600 tonnes on 630,600 m² (2025). Heating/lighting requires energy – link to waste heat or district heating.

food_e25.claim: Vertical farms/plant factories with artificial light require about 15.6–20.1 kWh of electricity per kg of lettuce depending on climate (lowest in cold regions, e.g. Reykjavik 15.6; highest in hot ones, e.g. the United Arab Emirates 20.1).
food_e25.context: Simulation of the same plant factory in different locations (Weidner et al. 2021), summarised in a review (Cai et al. 2024, arXiv preprint). Lighting and ventilation dominate. A later study by the same group (Nature Food 2022, nine urban regions including Stockholm) found that greenhouses have lower energy requirements per unit produced and, in most regions, the lowest land requirements when renewable electricity is included. Use as the electricity cost per kg for the vertical farming lever.

food_e26.claim: A mussel farm optimised for nutrient removal in a eutrophic Danish fjord produced 60 tonnes of mussels per hectare and removed 0.6–0.9 tonnes of nitrogen and 0.03–0.04 tonnes of phosphorus per hectare per year, at a cost of 14.8 euros per kg of nitrogen.
food_e26.context: The cost was competitive with the most expensive land-based measures. Should be seen as an upper reference value; in the brackish water of the Baltic Sea, growth and nutrient removal are much lower (food_e27, food_e38).

food_e27.claim: Along a salinity gradient in the German Baltic Sea (7–17 psu), 1 ha of mussel farming over six months yielded 1–51 tonnes of mussels and removed 24.7–612.7 kg of nitrogen and 1.1–27.7 kg of phosphorus; the cost of nitrogen removal was 162–4,018 euros per kg N.
food_e27.context: Four trial farms + a dynamic energy budget model. Growth increased with salinity; only saltier sites west of Rostock were profitable for food (2.2 €/kg), and no site was profitable for feed sales (0.06 €/kg). Low salinity (as in the Baltic Proper) gives the lowest values and the highest costs per kg N.

food_e28.claim: Farming and harvesting blue mussels in the central Baltic Sea can be a cost-effective complement to land-based measures against eutrophication, despite the mussels' low nutrient content; farming technique affects the cost more than nutrient content does, and current regulations are a bottleneck.
food_e28.context: Baltic-wide study (Baltic Blue Growth researchers). Mussels from the saltier outer Baltic Sea had higher N and P content.

food_e29.claim: Swedish farming of molluscs (mainly mussels and oysters) amounted to about 2,100 tonnes in 2025, spread across 9 companies (900 tonnes in 2024).
food_e29.context: Swedish Board of Agriculture aquaculture statistics. Shows that the sector is small and uneven from year to year; 'other organisms' (including algae) about 200 tonnes. Starting point for the mussel lever.

food_e30.claim: Regenerative maize farms in the northern US had 29% lower yields but 78% higher profits than conventional farms, and pests were ten times more common in insecticide-treated fields.
food_e30.context: Single study with farm-defined practices (cover crops, no tillage, grazing, no insecticides). Profit correlated with soil organic matter, not with yield. Shows the trade-off: better economics and ecosystem services but lower production per hectare – more land or a dietary shift is required.

food_e31.claim: Organic yields are on average lower than conventional yields: from 5% lower (rain-fed legumes and perennials) and 13% lower (best organic practices) to 34% lower when the systems are most comparable.
food_e31.context: Global meta-analysis. Used as a yield deduction when the player chooses a large-scale organic/agroecological transition. Compare Pittelkow et al. 2015 (Nature): no-till farming lowers yields, but least when combined with crop rotation and crop residues.

food_e32.claim: Catch crops (cover crops) increase soil carbon stocks by on average 0.32 ± 0.08 tonnes of carbon per hectare per year; a new equilibrium is reached after about 155 years, with a total of about 16.7 tonnes C/ha.
food_e32.context: Meta-analysis of 139 trial plots at 37 sites (0–22 cm). Corresponds to about 1.2 tonnes CO2/ha/year. Nitrous oxide and albedo not included.

food_e33.claim: When soil carbon saturation is taken into account, the possible climate contribution of soil carbon sequestration up to 2100 falls by 53–81%, and the effect of increased soil carbon on yields is inconsistent (negative to positive) across more than 21 meta-analyses.
food_e33.context: Critical review. Soil carbon should be seen as a co-benefit ('carbon for soils, not soils for carbon'), not as a primary climate measure. In the model: let carbon sequestration taper off towards saturation and do not give an automatic yield bonus.

food_e34.claim: Optimised school lunches in four Swedish schools (OPTIMAT) had a 28% lower climate impact and were slightly cheaper, with no significant change in how much the pupils ate or in plate waste.
food_e34.context: Linear programming with nutritional requirements and a cap of 500 g CO2e/meal; more legumes, cereals, eggs and non-ruminant meat, less beef, fat and sauces. Short intervention (3+3 weeks). Directly applicable to the public meals lever.

food_e35.claim: Experience from establishing edible forest gardens on 12 Swedish farms shows potential in multi-layered growing, but major knowledge gaps remain about production, economics and cultivation techniques; to contribute more than locally they must be scaled up, e.g. on marginal land and in transition zones.
food_e35.context: Participatory action research in Sweden. No reliable yield figures for forest gardens in a Nordic climate were found in this review – model forest gardens mainly as biodiversity, climate adaptation and social benefits, with low and uncertain food production (assumption).

food_e36.claim: Assumption: today's average Swedish diet requires about 0.45 ha of arable-land equivalents per person (range 0.35–0.6), while a planetary health diet with animals on pasture and leftovers requires about 0.2 ha (range 0.15–0.3).
food_e36.context: Model assumption, not measured. Derivation: Sweden has ~0.24 ha of arable land per inhabitant (food_e12) and produces roughly half of what is eaten (food_e16) → total land requirement including imports roughly 0.45 ha. The target diet is based on Peters et al. (food_e1–e2: 0.13 ha for a vegan diet, lower carrying capacity without pasture) and on plant-based diets saving up to 76% of land (food_e3); the Swedish diet exceeds the cropland boundary 2–4 times (food_e6). Calibrate against national calculations from SLU (Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences) if such are produced.

food_e39.claim: Sweden's national food strategy has as its overall objective a competitive food supply chain in which total food production increases while relevant national environmental objectives are achieved.
food_e39.context: The Swedish Board of Agriculture follows up the strategy annually. food_e13). No quantitative targets for self-sufficiency were found on the page.

food_e40.claim: If all suitable flat roofs in Bologna (Italy) were used for growing, they could produce just over 12,000 tonnes of vegetables per year, corresponding to around 77% of residents' vegetable needs.
food_e40.context: Based on rooftop growing trials in Bologna, a GIS mapping of flat roofs and residents' dietary needs. The figure is a technical maximum potential and does not take into account load-bearing capacity, ownership, economics or the winter season. The figures (>12,000 t/year, 77%) have been verified via summaries (the European Commission's 'Science for Environment Policy', according to TABLE, and search hits on the abstract). The abstract itself could not be opened. Use as an upper limit.

food_e41.claim: In a rooftop garden on a public housing apartment block in Bologna (2012–2014), tomatoes yielded 13–14 kg/m² and aubergines 8.2 kg/m² per season in soil. Other crops yielded less than 5 kg/m², and lettuce 1–1.3 kg/m² per growing cycle.
food_e41.context: Trial with life-cycle assessment in a shared rooftop garden. Growing in soil was cheapest and had the lowest climate impact for fruiting vegetables (about 74 g CO2 per kg for tomatoes and aubergines). Floating hydroponics was best for lettuce in summer. Growing was done as polyculture for household needs, which gave lower yields per area for some crops than in commercial monoculture. A reasonable range for open-air rooftop growing in southern Sweden is probably lower than for Bologna (assumption: 2–8 kg/m²).

food_e42.claim: Hydroponic lettuce growing in greenhouses is estimated to yield 41 ± 6.1 kg/m² per year versus 3.9 kg/m² in open fields, i.e. about 11 times more per area. However, it requires about 82 times more energy: 90,000 kJ (about 25 kWh) per kg versus 1,100 kJ per kg.
food_e42.context: Model calculation for Yuma, Arizona (USA). Water requirements were 20 L/kg versus 250 L/kg in open fields. Energy requirements are dominated by heating and cooling, and in a Swedish climate would mainly be heating and lighting in winter. The parameter illustrates the central dilemma for near-urban greenhouses and vertical farming: a lot of food per area, but high energy requirements (cf. food_e25 on vertical farming). Cheap waste heat, for example from combined heat and power plants or data centres, can change the calculation.

food_e43.claim: Aquaponics (fish farming in which the fish waste fertilises the plants) gave as much lettuce as pure hydroponics: 2.7 versus 2.8 kg/m² in the first growing cycle and 5.6–5.7 versus 6.0 kg/m² in the second.
food_e43.context: A single trial in Italy (Università della Tuscia) with tilapia at different stocking densities. The yield per year depends on the number of growing cycles, often 6–10 per year in a heated greenhouse. Aquaponics produces both fish and vegetables but is technically sensitive, and according to market studies few commercial facilities are highly profitable. In the model, aquaponics should be treated as a greenhouse technology with the yields and energy requirements of hydroponics (food_e42), plus a small fish production.

food_e44.claim: Sugar kelp (Saccharina latissima) requires a salinity above 23 psu for high yields and can therefore only be farmed in the westernmost parts of the Baltic Sea. Gut weed (Ulva intestinalis) and bladderwrack (Fucus vesiculosus), on the other hand, have farming potential in the southern and eastern Baltic Sea as well.
food_e44.context: Modelling of the farming potential for macroalgae across the whole Baltic Sea. The farms caused no significant nutrient depletion, and the impact spread less than 100–250 m. The spread was greater in nutrient-poor areas with little water exchange, such as the open sea of the Baltic Proper. food_e27, where the study's lowest salinity was 7 psu). It should be modelled as a small complement to mussel farming, not as a large nutrient trap.

food_e46.claim: The Swedish Board of Agriculture's 'supply capacity' (Swedish production as a share of consumption) in 2023: cereals about 105% (2023/24), drinking milk about 100%, dairy products overall 75% (cheese 39%), eggs 95%, carrots 97%, onions 78%, strawberries 69%, cucumbers 48%, apples 29% and tomatoes 19%.
food_e46.context: The Swedish Board of Agriculture deliberately presents no overall figure for Sweden. The agency points out that production depends on imported inputs (fertiliser, pesticides, feed, fuel, machinery and spare parts), so that actual self-sufficiency in a crisis is lower than these shares. The measure applies to fresh products, not processed or composite foods. It is suitable as starting values per food group in the model. Vegetables (especially greenhouse vegetables) are weakest and cereals strongest.

energy_e3.claim: At the end of 2025 there were about 314,600 grid-connected solar PV installations in Sweden with a total capacity of 5,541 MW.
energy_e3.context: Official statistics from the Swedish Energy Agency (published 7 April 2026). In 2025, 21,600 new installations were added (roughly half as many as in 2024), and total installed capacity increased by approx. 15% compared with 2024. Over a year, the total capacity corresponds to roughly the electricity use of Halland County, or approx. 13.4% of household electricity use. Trend: 4,800 MW at the end of 2024, and the record year 2023 with 1.6 GW of new capacity. Growth is sensitive to electricity prices and interest rates.

energy_e5.claim: An estimated 650–800 MW of battery capacity was installed in Sweden in 2024, often together with solar PV for self-consumption and flexibility services.
energy_e5.context: Estimate in the Swedish Energy Agency's Swedish-language summary of the IEA PVPS National Survey Report for 2024. Driven by the tax reduction for green technology. Shows that local storage is already scaling up in Sweden; useful as a growth parameter for household and building batteries.

energy_e7.claim: On 4 November 2024 the Government rejected thirteen offshore wind farms in the Baltic Sea on defence grounds; according to the Government, wind farms can halve the time available to detect incoming cruise missiles, from 2 minutes to 60 seconds.
energy_e7.context: Rejected wind farms: Arkona, Aurora, Baltic Offshore Beta, Baltic Offshore Delta North, Cirrus, Dyning, Erik Segersäll, Neptunus, Pleione, Skidbladner, Skåne Havsvindpark, Södra Victoria and Triton. At the same time, Poseidon (west coast, up to 5.5 TWh/year) was granted a permit.

energy_e9.claim: In 2024 the global weighted average levelised cost of electricity (LCOE) was 0.043 USD/kWh for new solar power, 0.034 USD/kWh for onshore wind and 0.079 USD/kWh for offshore wind (Europe 0.080 USD/kWh).
energy_e9.context: IRENA's annual cost report. Onshore wind was 53% cheaper and solar power 41% cheaper than the cheapest fossil alternative; 91% of new renewable capacity in 2024 was cheaper than new fossil capacity. Costs rose slightly in 2023–2024 (solar +0.6%, onshore wind +3%, offshore wind +4%) after large declines since 2010 (solar LCOE −90% in 2010–2023 according to IRENA's report for 2023). In the EU, solar LCOE rose because of permitting processes and grid connection. Use as a relative cost ranking; Swedish levels differ (lower solar irradiance, higher labour costs).

energy_e10.claim: The total installed cost of utility-scale battery storage fell by 93% between 2010 and 2024, from 2,571 to 192 USD/kWh.
energy_e10.context: IRENA 2025. Solar-plus-battery hybrid projects (17 projects in 2024) reached 0.079 USD/kWh, on a par with combined-cycle gas power plants. Model parameter for cost learning: approx. −17% per year on average in 2010–2024 (derived: (192/2571)^(1/14) ≈ 0.83). The future rate is uncertain.

energy_e11.claim: The price of lithium-ion battery packs fell by 20% in 2024 to a record-low global average of 115 USD/kWh.
energy_e11.context: BloombergNEF's annual price survey (10 Dec 2024). Europe was approx. 48% above China (94 USD/kWh). Electric-vehicle packs dropped below 100 USD/kWh (97 USD/kWh). Relevant for electric cars, vehicle-to-grid (V2G) and building batteries.

energy_e12.claim: Heat pumps are three to five times more energy efficient than gas boilers, and in Sweden over 40% of buildings have a heat pump.
energy_e12.context: IEA's global heat pump report: “Heat pumps currently available on the market are three-to-five times more energy efficient than natural gas boilers” and “In Norway, 60% of buildings are equipped with heat pumps, with Sweden and Finland at over 40%”. Heinrich-Böll-Stiftung (2025, with EHPA data) reports approx. 50 heat pumps per 100 households in Sweden in 2024.

energy_e16.claim: Svenska kraftnät expects Sweden's electricity use to rise from 138 TWh (2022) to just over 340 TWh in 2045 in the two most likely electrification scenarios.
energy_e16.context: Långsiktig marknadsanalys 2024 (LMA2024, long-term market analysis). Four scenarios for 2050: Small-scale renewables 210 TWh, Mixed roadmap 265 TWh, Electrification dispatchable 365 TWh, Electrification renewables 365 TWh. “These are not forecasts.” The increase is driven mainly by industry (steel). Model implication: competition for electricity and grid capacity raises electricity prices and the value of local generation and energy efficiency.

energy_e17.claim: The European federation of citizen-owned energy cooperatives represents over 2,250 cooperatives and 1.5 million citizens; according to a study cited by the European Commission, approx. 45% of the EU's renewable energy production could come from citizens in 2050.
energy_e17.context: The European Commission's Sustainable Energy Week (March 2024), with figures from REScoop.eu. The legal basis is the EU Renewable Energy Directive (RED II, renewable energy communities) and the Electricity Market Directive (citizen energy communities). The 45% figure comes from CE Delft and is an assessment of potential, not a forecast.

energy_e20.claim: Assumption: 1 kWp of modern solar panels requires about 5 m² of roof area.
energy_e20.context: Physically derived: kWp is defined at an irradiance of 1,000 W/m²; with a module efficiency of approx. 20–22%, 4.5–5 m² of module area is needed per kWp, plus margins for edges, shading and fire access paths. Combined with energy_e1 this gives approx. Not directly verified against a source in this compilation – check against manufacturer data.

mobility_e4.claim: In 2025, 3.8 billion trips were made in Sweden, of which about 1,946 million by car (approx. 51%), 707 million by public transport and 560 million on foot.
mobility_e4.context: Trafikanalys (Transport Analysis), Resvanor i Sverige 2025 (official statistics, ages 6–84, approx. 14,500 respondents, published 28 May 2026). Shares calculated by the compiler from the number of trips. Walking trips increased by 12% and car trips decreased by 5% compared with 2024; cycling trips decreased by 1% (the cycling share is not given in the retrieved text).

mobility_e5.claim: Regular cycling equivalent to 11.25 MET-hours per week (roughly 100 minutes) reduces the risk of premature death from all causes by 10%; the corresponding figure for walking is 11%.
mobility_e5.context: Systematic review and meta-analysis (cycling: 7 studies, 187,000 people; walking: 14 studies, 280,000 people), adjusted for other physical activity. The effect is greatest at low levels – getting inactive people to start cycling yields the most. This is the dose–response relationship used in the WHO HEAT tool for health economic assessment. Use as the dose–response in the model's health module.

mobility_e6.claim: People who commuted by bicycle had a 41% lower risk of death from all causes, a 46% lower risk of cardiovascular disease and a 45% lower risk of cancer compared with those who commuted by car or public transport.
mobility_e6.context: Prospective cohort study, UK Biobank, 263,450 participants, median follow-up 5 years. HR 0.59 (all-cause mortality), 0.54 (cardiovascular disease, incidence), 0.55 (cancer incidence). Walking to work: HR 0.73 for cardiovascular disease but no significant effect on all-cause mortality. Observational study – causality is probably overestimated (healthier people cycle more); use mobility_e5 as the more cautious main parameter.

mobility_e7.claim: Implementing 503 superblocks in Barcelona is estimated to prevent 667 premature deaths per year, give adults an average of almost 200 days' longer life expectancy and yield an annual economic benefit of EUR 1.7 billion.
mobility_e7.context: Quantitative health impact assessment (modelling, not measured outcomes). Largest contributions: reduced NO2 (291), noise (163), heat (117), green space (60), increased physical activity (36). Approx. 51 deaths per 100,000 adults per year.

mobility_e8.claim: Since 1999, Pontevedra (Spain, approx. 84,000 inhabitants) has handed back to pedestrians approx. 80% of the street space that was allocated to motor vehicles. Motor traffic has fallen by 92% in the historic city centre, 77% in the centre and 53% in the outer district (ensanche).
mobility_e8.context: The municipality's own figures, published in the Spanish Directorate-General for Traffic's (DGT) catalogue of good practice (NIPO 128-22-050-6, approx. 2022). It also states that 66% of internal trips are made on foot, 5% by bicycle or public transport and 28% by car. Seriously injured road casualties fell from 129 in 1999 to 4 in 2020. No road deaths are reported for 12 years from 2007. The European Commission reports zero deaths in 2011–2018 (see mobility_e18). The figures have not been independently evaluated. The previously often-cited figure of 67% lower CO2 emissions could not be verified in a primary source and is not used.

mobility_e9.claim: Oslo removed 760 parking spaces in the city centre inside Ring 1 under the Car-free City Life programme (Bilfritt byliv) 2016–2023 and replaced them with seating, greenery, bicycle parking and activities.
mobility_e9.context: Oslo Municipality's programme page (accessed 2026; the programme ran 2016–2023). The programme chose to remove parking and through traffic rather than ban cars entirely; goods deliveries and parking for people with reduced mobility were retained. Quantitative effects on retail are reported in separate “Byregnskap” (city accounts) that have not been reviewed here.

mobility_e10.claim: Ghent's Circulation Plan (April 2017) divided the inner city into sectors without through traffic for cars. After a year and a half, the number of cars entering and leaving the inner city had fallen by an average of 17%, while the number of cyclists had increased by approx. 50% within the inner city and approx. 60% to and from it.
mobility_e10.context: The city's evaluation (measurements April–November 2018, carried out together with Transport & Mobility Leuven). The modal split of Ghent residents changed as follows between 2015 and 2018: car as driver 40 → 33%, bicycle 30 → 35%, public transport 9 → 14% and walking 15 → 13%. The car-free area increased from 22.4 to 51.2 ha (2.9 → 6.5% of the inner city). Public transport use rose by 6% per day but fell by 9% in the morning rush hour. The plan was implemented with relatively cheap means (signs, barriers, cameras). The effect can therefore be used as a benchmark for a quick, cheap measure: −15 to −20% car traffic in the centre within 1–2 years.

mobility_e11.claim: More than 70 case studies from eleven countries show that when street space is reallocated from car traffic to walking, cycling and public transport, the feared traffic problems are often considerably smaller than expected – some of the traffic “disappears”.
mobility_e11.context: Cairns, Atkins & Goodwin (2002), summary of two research phases and a survey of more than 200 transport experts. The effect size varies with local conditions; the abstract gives no single figure. In modelling terms: traffic volume is not constant – reduced road capacity leads to some reduction in total traffic (an elasticity assumption should be stated separately).

mobility_e12.claim: In outer London areas where Low Traffic Neighbourhoods were introduced, car ownership and car use fell and active travel increased more than in comparison areas.
mobility_e12.context: Aldred & Goodman (2020), panel study 2016–2019 in Outer London. The small sample size in LTN areas makes the effect size uncertain, but the direction is consistent. Reduced car ownership was seen only in areas with LTNs – not from cycle lanes alone.

mobility_e13.claim: In Copenhagen, two thirds of shopping trips and half of shops' turnover come from customers who walk or cycle; retailers often overestimate how many customers arrive by car.
mobility_e13.context: Compiled in Transport for London's evidence review (2018), citing the Copenhagen Bicycle Account 2012 and O'Connor et al. 2011 respectively (retailers on two shopping streets overestimated car-borne customers and underestimated cyclists).

mobility_e14.claim: The “15-minute city” (Carlos Moreno, 2016) means that residents should be able to reach their everyday needs – work, shopping, healthcare, school, culture and recreation – within 15 minutes on foot or by bicycle (“chrono-urbanism”).
mobility_e14.context: A concept paper, not an impact study: the empirical evidence for the health and climate effects of 15-minute planning is still limited, and the concept has been criticised for potentially driving gentrification and for suiting rural areas less well. Use as a planning indicator (share of inhabitants with services within 15 min).

mobility_e15.claim: In Augustenborg in Malmö, 90% of stormwater from roofs and hard surfaces is channelled into open ditches and ponds, reducing annual runoff to the drainage network by about 20%; the area came through the cloudbursts of 2007 and 2014 without flood damage.
mobility_e15.context: EU Climate-ADAPT case study (2017). More than 11,000 m² of green roofs (of which 9,000 m² is a botanical roof garden); total investment approx. EUR 24 million (approx. SEK 200 million) in 1998–2002, of which the housing company MKB paid roughly half. During a 50-year rainfall event in 2007, large parts of Malmö were affected but not Augustenborg; in 2014 (over 100 mm in 6 hours) there was no local damage. Model parameter for de-paving and blue-green solutions.

mobility_e16.claim: The 2011 cloudburst in Copenhagen caused damage of more than 6 billion Danish kroner; the city's cloudburst plan with surface solutions (streets as channels, parks as detention areas) was estimated to cost approx. DKK 12 billion, compared with DKK 20 billion for a purely pipe-based solution.
mobility_e16.context: Climate-ADAPT case study. The plan comprises approx. 300 projects (approx. 15 per year over 20–30 years). The combined solution gave an estimated net gain of approx. DKK 3 billion, while the traditional solution gave a net loss of approx. DKK 4 billion. Shows that surface solutions can be both cheaper and provide added value (greenery, recreation).

mobility_e18.claim: Pontevedra received the EU's first Urban Road Safety Award (2020). According to the Commission, the local police recorded no road deaths in 2011–2018, and 80% of children aged 6–12 walk to school on their own.
mobility_e18.context: The European Commission's (DG Mobility and Transport) citation, 18 May 2020. Measures included speed limits of 10–30 km/h and attractive public spaces for pedestrians. The share of children who walk to school on their own is a good indicator for the game of how independent children are and how safe the streets are.

mobility_e19.claim: Retail in Ghent after the Circulation Plan: 30% of Ghent residents said they shop less often in the inner city, 65% that it had not affected them and 5% that they shop more often. At the same time, new retail and hospitality (horeca) businesses in the centre increased by 20% (2018 compared with 2017), and closures and bankruptcies fell by 7%.
mobility_e19.context: Survey (mobility survey) and business data (Graydon) in the city's 2019 evaluation. The evaluators point out that answers about shopping “less often” cannot be translated directly into an equally large loss of turnover. The business data show no hampered growth in the centre. A good basis for a trade-off in the game: retailers' concerns are real and measurable in surveys, but the structural effect on the business community was not negative.

community_e1.claim: People with stronger social relationships have a 50% higher likelihood of surviving over the follow-up period than people with weak relationships.
community_e1.context: Meta-analysis of 148 prospective studies with 308,849 participants (mean follow-up 7.5 years). The effect was consistent across age, sex, health status and cause of death. Used as the base parameter for how a 'social network index' affects mortality in the model; observational data, so causality is not fully established.

community_e2.claim: Perceived loneliness increases mortality by an average of 26%.
community_e2.context: Meta-analysis of 70 prospective studies (approx. 3.4 million participants) in which confounders were controlled for. Same study: social isolation OR 1.29 and living alone OR 1.32 (see community_e3). Suitable as a risk multiplier in the model's mortality calculation for the share of the population reporting loneliness.

community_e3.claim: Objective social isolation increases mortality by 29% and living alone by 32%.
community_e3.context: From the same meta-analysis as community_e2: social isolation OR 1.29; living alone OR 1.32. Objective isolation and subjective loneliness are different mechanisms – the model can use both.

community_e4.claim: Loneliness is linked to an estimated 871,000 deaths a year worldwide (about 100 per hour); one in six people is affected by loneliness.
community_e4.context: WHO Commission on Social Connection (report, June 2025). In high-income countries about 11% say they feel lonely (versus about 24% in low-income countries). Lonely teenagers are 22% more likely to get lower grades; lonely people are twice as likely to become depressed. Provides global context and supports treating social connection as a public health issue; the World Health Assembly adopted a resolution on social connection in May 2025.

community_e5.claim: About 664,000 people in Sweden (aged 16+) have no close friend, 7–8% of the population.
community_e5.context: Statistics Sweden (SCB) Living Conditions Surveys (ULF) 2023, confidence interval 610,000–720,000 people. Men 9.4%, women 6.1%; foreign-born 13.1% versus 6.2% for Swedish-born; less than upper secondary education 12.2% versus 5.2% for post-secondary education; 65+ 8.0%.

community_e6.claim: 26% of adults in Sweden (28% of women, 24% of men) are mildly or severely troubled by loneliness or isolation; about 3% are severely troubled.
community_e6.context: National Public Health Survey 2022, reported in the Public Health Agency of Sweden's 2024 mapping. Highest among 16–29-year-olds and those aged 85+. People living alone 47% versus those living with others 21%. Severely troubled: 2% among those in work, 11% among the unemployed and 14% among those on long-term sick leave. In ULF 2022, 8% said they feel lonely most or all of the time (14% among the oldest). The Public Health Agency of Sweden estimates involuntary loneliness at about 6% of the population. Starting value for the model's loneliness indicator.

community_e7.claim: Among people troubled by loneliness, 24% have serious psychological distress, compared with 4% among those who are not troubled; 28% versus 9% have had suicidal thoughts.
community_e7.context: National Public Health Survey 2022. Share in good general health: 56% among the lonely versus 78% among the non-lonely; good mental well-being 65% versus 93%. Cross-sectional data – the association probably runs in both directions. Links the community indicator to the health indicator in the model.

community_e8.claim: 41% of all households in Sweden consist of one person.
community_e8.context: Statistics Sweden (SCB) population statistics 2022, cited in the Public Health Agency of Sweden's loneliness mapping. The share of single-person households is higher in older age groups.

community_e9.claim: In residential care homes (säbo) with daily activities, 17% often feel lonely, compared with 36% where activities are offered less than once a month.
community_e9.context: National Board of Health and Welfare survey 'Vad tycker de äldre om äldreomsorgen?' (What do older people think of elderly care?), reported by the Public Health Agency of Sweden in 2024. Overall, 19% in residential care homes and 12% receiving home care say they are often troubled by loneliness. Cross-sectional comparison (may be affected by other differences between the homes), but gives a reasonable upper bound for what the range of activities offered in municipal elderly care can influence.

community_e10.claim: The 1995 Chicago heat wave killed 739 people in one week; mortality was roughly ten times higher in North Lawndale than in the neighbouring district of Little Village, which had similar levels of poverty but a stronger social life.
community_e10.context: Klinenberg's 'social autopsy' showed that many died alone at home and that differences in social infrastructure (shops, street life, associations, density) explained part of the differences between neighbourhoods. The figure of 40 versus 4 deaths per 100,000 inhabitants is taken from secondary summaries of the book. Klinenberg developed the concept of social infrastructure (libraries, parks, meeting places) in 'Palaces for the People' (2018).

community_e11.claim: Restoring vacant lots (clean-up, grass, trees, fencing) reduced gun violence by 29% in poor neighbourhoods and increased the use of outdoor spaces for socialising by 76%.
community_e11.context: Cluster-randomised study in Philadelphia with 541 lots and 445 residents interviewed over 38 months. Also reduced perceived crime (−36.8%) and fear of going outside (−57.8%). A cheap, scalable 'social infrastructure' measure.

community_e12.claim: Eight out of ten studies examining health and well-being in cohousing found a positive association, but the quality of the evidence is low.
community_e12.context: Scoping review: 2,560 articles screened, 25 included, analysing 77 housing examples, all in high-income countries. 22 studies on psychosocial determinants of health (social support, community, safety) – most of them positive. Mostly cross-sectional and qualitative studies; selection effects (those who choose cohousing are already sociable) cannot be ruled out. The model should therefore use a small effect size.

community_e13.claim: The Färdknäppen cohousing building in Stockholm ('the second half of life') has 43 flats of 37–75 m² and about 400 m² of shared space, with shared dinners cooked by rotating cooking teams.
community_e13.context: Initiated in 1993 together with the municipal housing company Familjebostäder. Gives a design parameter: about 9 m² of shared space per flat. Facts from the CO-HOPE research project (TU Wien) and an architecture database.

community_e14.claim: The Humanitas care home in Deventer (the Netherlands) lets students live rent-free in return for spending at least 30 hours a month being 'good neighbours' to the older residents.
community_e14.context: Running since around 2013; a handful of students among about 160 older residents according to press reports. No published impact evaluation found – the example is an inspirational model for intergenerational housing, not a proven effect.

community_e15.claim: Ostrom's design principles for governing the commons have strong empirical support in a review of 91 studies.
community_e15.context: Ostrom (1990, Governing the Commons) formulated eight principles (clear boundaries, locally adapted rules, participation in rule-making, monitoring, graduated sanctions, conflict resolution, recognised right to self-determination, nested levels). Cox et al. found the principles well supported and proposed a refined version with ten principles. Used as a qualitative basis for the game's 'commons' (allotment gardens, tool libraries, energy communities, fishing waters).

community_e16.claim: Ireland's Citizens' Assembly (99 randomly selected citizens) proposed changing the abortion ban; the referendum on 25 May 2018 returned 66.4% yes.
community_e16.context: The assembly (2016–2018) considered five issues (including the ageing population and climate) and met at weekends. Its recommendations went via a parliamentary committee to a referendum. In the assembly, 64% supported abortion without restrictions. An example of how randomly selected assemblies can break political deadlock – but the effect depends on a clear link to decision-making.

community_e17.claim: France's Citizens' Convention for Climate: 150 randomly selected citizens drew up 149 proposals, but the link to implementation was weak and support among the wider public was low.
community_e17.context: Giraudet et al. show that the steering committee's influence did not erode the citizens' freedom of action, but that the process did not create broad support outside the convention and that the commitment on how the proposals would be handled was too weak. The President promised to take forward 146 of the proposals; reviews (e.g. Reporterre) have claimed that only about 10% were implemented unchanged – the figure is disputed (verified only via secondary sources). Warns of 'cherry-picking' – a risk the model should include.

community_e18.claim: In Gdańsk, citizens' assembly proposals with at least 80% support become binding on the city; the first assembly (about 60 people, four Saturdays), on flooding after the 2016 cloudburst, produced 16 proposals.
community_e18.context: Mayor Adamowicz committed to implementing proposals with ≥80% support. The proposals included investment in monitoring and stormwater infrastructure (nearly USD 40 million according to the article), grants to property owners for local stormwater management and an information campaign. The source is an opinion piece (grey literature).

community_e19.claim: The OECD has mapped 289 representative deliberative processes (citizens' assemblies, juries, panels) from 1986–2019, with a clear increase after 2010.
community_e19.context: 282 of the cases were in OECD countries. The report identifies twelve models, good-practice principles and three routes to institutionalising citizen deliberation. Used as support for the view that randomly selected citizens' assemblies are an established, not experimental, form of democracy.

community_e20.claim: Brazilian municipalities with participatory budgeting directed more money to sanitation and health and saw infant mortality fall by about 1–3 per 1,000 (roughly 10–20%).
community_e20.context: Panel data for Brazilian municipalities 1990–2004. The effect sizes (1–3 per 1,000; budget share for health and sanitation +1.2 percentage points) are taken from the author's working paper (LSE 2009); the published version confirms the direction. Touchton & Wampler (2014, Comparative Political Studies) found similar associations that grow stronger the longer participatory budgeting has been in place. Transferability to a Swedish context with low infant mortality is limited – the mechanism (resources directed to needs that would otherwise be overlooked) is what is relevant.

community_e21.claim: Paris allocates 5% of the city's investment budget, about EUR 100 million a year, to participatory budgeting; in 2019, 231,822 people voted.
community_e21.context: About EUR 0.5 billion over the 2014–2020 term of office. 2019: 2,084 projects submitted, 196 winners, including an earmarked share for disadvantaged neighbourhoods and one for schools.

community_e22.claim: In the 2022 UK four-day week trial (61 companies, about 2,900 employees), 56 companies (92%) continued after the trial and staff turnover fell by 57%.
community_e22.context: The 100-80-100 model (full pay, 80% of the time, maintained productivity), June–December 2022. 18 companies made the change permanent; 71% reported lower burnout, 39% less stress; sick days fell by about 65% (figure from secondary summaries). Voluntary participation and no control group – the effects are probably overestimated for a whole labour market.

community_e23.claim: Iceland's working-time trials of 2015–2019 covered about 2,500 employees (over 1% of the workforce) on a 35–36-hour week without pay cuts; since then 86% of the workforce have gained shorter hours or the right to them.
community_e23.context: Trials in the City of Reykjavík and the state sector. Productivity and service provision were maintained or improved in most workplaces; well-being increased; cost-neutral according to the report. The report was written by advocacy think tanks – hence medium confidence.

community_e24.claim: The six-hour-day trial at the Svartedalen care home for older people in Gothenburg (2015–2017) cost about SEK 12 million for 17 extra staff; sick days fell by 4.7% while those in the control group rose by 62.5%.
community_e24.context: 68 assistant nurses moved to six-hour days on full pay. Staff reported better health and the quality of care improved; the trial was ended because permanent introduction was considered too expensive. The net cost (taking into account reduced unemployment and sickness absence) was not fully calculated. SVT (2015) instead gave SEK 8 million a year and 14 new hires early in the trial – the figures differ between sources.

community_e25.claim: The London time bank network valued its social value for 2015–2017 at about GBP 3.1 million against a budget of about GBP 0.3 million (roughly 10:1).
community_e25.context: Valued using HACT's Social Value tool across 14 outcomes (including relief from depression/anxiety and good health). Members report reduced loneliness and a greater sense of belonging. The evaluation was carried out by the umbrella organisation itself, without a control group – the ratio is a rough indication, not an effect. British research (Naughton-Doe et al. 2021) points to implementation problems: safety bureaucracy, professional paternalism and the need for resources for coordinators.

community_e26.claim: Assumption: A strong and sustained municipal programme for social infrastructure and community housing can reduce the share of adults troubled by loneliness by 2–5 percentage points (from about 26%) and the share with no close friend by 1–2 percentage points over 10–20 years.
community_e26.context: Model assumption. Reasoning: the difference between residential care homes with and without daily activities (17% versus 36%, community_e9) shows that environment and activities matter, but applies to a small group; cohousing studies show positive but weak associations (community_e12); loneliness is strongly linked to unemployment and income (community_e6), which the municipality can only partly influence. No population study shows how much a municipality can reduce loneliness – hence a cautious effect and a time lag. The mortality effect is calculated via OR 1.26 (community_e2).

health_e1.claim: Spending at least 120 minutes a week in nature is associated with a 59% higher likelihood of reporting good health and a 23% higher likelihood of high well-being.
health_e1.context: n = 19,806, representative English survey (MENE 2014–2016). Well-being OR 1.23 (1.08–1.40). The effect levels off at 200–300 min/week; no effect below 120 min. It also applied to older people and people with long-term illness; it made no difference whether the time was spent in one visit or several. Cross-sectional study – reverse causality possible. Model parameter: share of inhabitants reaching ≥120 min/week.

health_e2.claim: Children who grow up with the least greenery around their homes have up to 55% higher risk of psychiatric disorders later in life than those with the most greenery.
health_e2.context: Danish register study, about 1 million people; greenery measured by satellite (NDVI) within 210×210 m around the home from birth to age 10. The association remained after adjustment for urbanisation, socio-economic status and parental mental illness; cumulative exposure throughout childhood mattered most. 'Up to' – the effect varies between diagnoses. A strong argument for greenery at preschools, schools and homes.

health_e3.claim: Greater exposure to green space is associated with 31% lower all-cause mortality, 28% lower risk of type 2 diabetes and 16% lower cardiovascular mortality.
health_e3.context: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 103 observational and 40 intervention studies, about 100 health outcomes. Type 2 diabetes OR 0.72 (0.61–0.85); cardiovascular mortality OR 0.84 (0.76–0.93); preterm birth OR 0.87; diastolic blood pressure −1.97 mmHg; heart rate −2.57 beats/min; lower cortisol. The authors particularly recommend investment in socio-economically disadvantaged areas.

health_e4.claim: WHO Europe proposes as an indicator that everyone should live within 300 metres in a straight line (about a 5-minute walk) of a green space of at least 0.5 hectares (alternatively 1 hectare).
health_e4.context: The report summarises evidence for improved mental health, reduced cardiovascular disease, obesity and type 2 diabetes, and better pregnancy outcomes, via stress reduction, physical activity, and reduced air pollution, noise and heat. 0.5 ha is the core indicator, 1 ha an additional indicator.

health_e5.claim: Greening vacant lots reduced feelings of depression among nearby residents by 41.5%, and by 68.7% in neighbourhoods below the poverty line.
health_e5.context: Cluster-randomised study in Philadelphia, 541 lots, 342 participants with follow-up. Feelings of worthlessness −50.9%. A simple, cheap measure (clean-up, grass, trees, fencing, maintenance). Shows that even small green spaces in the local environment affect mental health – especially where needs are greatest.

health_e6.claim: The WHO recommends that adults do 150–300 minutes a week of moderate-intensity physical activity (or 75–150 minutes of vigorous-intensity activity) and that children and young people are active for an average of 60 minutes a day.
health_e6.context: WHO guidelines 2020; muscle-strengthening activity is recommended for all ages and sedentary time should be reduced. Used as the threshold for the model indicator 'share meeting recommended physical activity levels'.

health_e7.claim: Physical inactivity causes about 9% of all premature deaths worldwide (over 5.3 of 57 million deaths in 2008); eliminating inactivity would increase life expectancy by 0.68 years.
health_e7.context: The Lancet series on physical activity. A 10% reduction in inactivity would prevent over 533,000 deaths a year globally, and a 25% reduction over 1.3 million. Model parameter: life expectancy gain of up to about 0.7 years with full activity (0.41–0.95), scaled by the change in the share of inactive people.

health_e8.claim: Only about one in five Swedish schoolchildren (aged 11–15) is sufficiently physically active (at least 60 minutes a day).
health_e8.context: Skolbarns hälsovanor 2021/2022 (the Swedish part of the WHO Health Behaviour in School-aged Children study, HBSC). The next survey, 2025/2026, will be published in 2026–2027. The Public Health Agency of Sweden notes that sedentary behaviour is increasing in all age groups.

health_e9.claim: 77% of 15-year-old girls and 46% of 15-year-old boys have at least two psychosomatic complaints more than once a week – the highest level since measurements began in the 1980s.
health_e9.context: Skolbarns hälsovanor 2021/2022: 13-year-old girls 68%, boys 39%; 15-year-old girls 77%, boys 46%. Complaints = e.g. headache, stomach ache, feeling low, irritability, nervousness, difficulty sleeping. The share has gradually increased since the mid-1980s. A central indicator for young people's mental health in the model.

health_e10.claim: 19% of girls and 10% of boys aged 11–15 feel lonely most of the time or always.
health_e10.context: Skolbarns hälsovanor, reported in the Public Health Agency of Sweden's 2024 loneliness mapping. The share is lowest among 11-year-olds and highest among 15-year-olds. Links young people's mental health to the community theme (see community_e6).

health_e11.claim: Cycling to work is associated with 41% lower all-cause mortality, 45% lower risk of cancer and 46% lower risk of cardiovascular disease.
health_e11.context: UK Biobank, 263,450 participants. Cycle commuting: cardiovascular disease HR 0.54, cancer incidence HR 0.55, cancer mortality HR 0.60. Walking to work: lower cardiovascular disease (HR 0.73) but no significant effect on all-cause mortality. Observational study. Links the mobility theme to health.

health_e12.claim: Public health interventions in high-income countries return a median of 14 times the money invested (ROI 14.3:1); local interventions 4.1:1 and national ones (e.g. legislation) 27.2:1.
health_e12.context: Systematic review of 52 studies. Median benefit–cost ratio 8.3. The authors conclude that cuts to public health budgets are a 'false economy'. For a municipality, the ROI of 4.1:1 for local interventions is the most relevant parameter; the benefits often accrue to other bodies (the region, the state) and with a delay.

health_e15.claim: About 130,000–150,000 people in Sweden have dementia (2023), 20,000–25,000 develop it each year, and the number is expected to reach 230,000–270,000 by 2050.
health_e15.context: The cost to society was estimated in 2023 at about SEK 90–100 billion a year, of which SEK 81–84.5 billion is borne by the municipalities (mainly elderly care), SEK 1.3 billion by the regions and SEK 11.4–14.4 billion by relatives providing informal care. This is why dementia is the heaviest ageing-related item in the municipal budget in the model. Physical activity, social connection and blood pressure control are commonly cited as preventive factors (not quantified here).

health_e16.claim: 70% of Sweden's population feel they are in good health, but health inequalities between socio-economic groups are widening in several areas.
health_e16.context: The Public Health Agency of Sweden's follow-up 'Folkhälsan i Sverige – årsrapport 2025' (page updated March 2026). The national goal is to close the avoidable health gaps within a generation.

health_e17.claim: Assumption: In the model, every 10-percentage-point increase in the share of inhabitants getting ≥120 minutes in nature per week increases the share with good self-rated health by about 0.5–1 percentage point.
health_e17.context: Model assumption. Derived from White et al. (health_e1): OR 1.59 for good health at 120–179 min versus 0 min. With a baseline of about 70% in good health (health_e16), OR 1.59 corresponds to a difference of roughly 9 percentage points between the groups; we halve the effect to allow for reverse causality (healthy people go outdoors more) and because not everyone starts from 0 min. 10% of the population × about 4.5–9 p.p. ≈ 0.5–1 p.p. in total. Should be recalibrated if Swedish longitudinal data become available.

digital_resilience_e1.claim: The state set aside SEK 685 million in 2023 and SEK 658 million in 2024 in government grants for textbooks and teachers’ guides, and estimates just over SEK 0.5 billion per year from 2025, with the goal of “one textbook per pupil and subject”.
digital_resilience_e1.context: A government grant that head teachers apply for, covering preschool class, compulsory school, adapted compulsory school, special school and Sami school. The Government argues that basic skills are best developed in analogue environments with analogue tools.

digital_resilience_e2.claim: In its 2023 consultation response to the Swedish National Agency for Education’s proposed national digitalisation strategy, Karolinska Institutet wrote that there is clear scientific evidence that digital tools impair rather than enhance pupils’ learning, and advocated printed textbooks and teachers’ expertise.
digital_resilience_e2.context: The statement is dated 28 April 2023 and was written by professors Lisa Thorell, Torkel Klingberg, Agneta Herlitz, Andreas Olsson and Ulrika Ådén. As an example, it notes that students with an internet-connected computer spent up to 40% of lecture time on unrelated activities (Kraushaar & Novak 2010). The often-quoted statement in English translation via AP/VOA reads: “There's clear scientific evidence that digital tools impair rather than enhance student learning.” KI’s own statement (ki.se/media/260512/download) requires a login and could not be opened. It has therefore been verified via secondary sources (AP/VOA and search results on the statement’s content), so the exact Swedish wording has not been checked. The statement is contested: critics argue that the effect depends on how the technology is used. Use it as a political driver, not as an effect size.

digital_resilience_e3.claim: Swedish 15-year-olds scored 482 points in mathematics (−21 compared with 2018) and 487 in reading comprehension (−19) in PISA 2022; science 494 (−6, within the margin of error).
digital_resilience_e3.context: The decline was larger than the OECD average (approx. −15 in mathematics, −10 in reading) and brought Sweden back close to its 2012 low point. The causes are debated (screens, the pandemic, pupil composition); use as the starting point for the ‘basic skills’ indicator, not as proof of the effect of screens. Figures verified via The Local, citing the OECD country report (the OECD page blocked automated retrieval).

digital_resilience_e4.claim: The Public Health Agency of Sweden’s recommendations (Sept 2024) for leisure screen use: children under 2 should as far as possible not use screens, ages 2–5 at most 1 hour/day, ages 6–12 at most 1–2 hours/day, ages 13–18 at most 2–3 hours/day; no screens before bedtime and phones kept out of the bedroom at night.
digital_resilience_e4.context: Applies to leisure time (social media, video, TV, gaming) – not schoolwork, music, podcasts or e-books. Justified by links to poorer sleep and depressive symptoms. Model parameter: the share of children who follow the guidelines can be used as an indicator of ‘screen balance’. Figures verified via Sveriges Radio and communications from the Public Health Agency of Sweden and the Government (the press release of 2 Sept 2024 refers to the FoHM website).

digital_resilience_e5.claim: On 21 May 2026 the Riksdag decided (committee report 2025/26:UbU22, Government bill 2025/26:193) that pupils’ mobile phones are to be collected at the start of the school day and returned at its end in compulsory school, adapted compulsory school, special school, Sami school, school-age educare and open leisure activities. The law applies from 1 August 2026.
digital_resilience_e5.context: Exceptions: educational use as instructed by the teacher, additional adaptations/special support, special reasons for an individual pupil, and outdoor teaching. The bill mentions ‘certain financial consequences for the municipalities’ (storage, staff time) without giving an exact amount. Upper secondary school is not covered. In the game this is a national constraint from 2026 – the municipality’s choice concerns how far beyond the law to go (e.g. upper secondary school, screen-free breaks).

digital_resilience_e6.claim: After schools in four English cities banned mobile phones, pupils’ results in final exams rose by an average of about 0.07 standard deviations, driven by the lowest-performing pupils.
digital_resilience_e6.context: Difference-in-differences across 91 schools (Birmingham, London, Leicester, Manchester), 16-year-olds. Often cited as ‘6.4% of a standard deviation’. The effect is small on average but larger for weaker pupils – relevant to equality indicators. English context 2001–2011; transferability to Sweden is uncertain.

digital_resilience_e7.claim: A British study of 1,227 pupils (aged 12–15) in 30 schools found no difference in mental well-being (WEMWBS, p=0.62) between schools with restrictive and permissive phone policies. Pupils in restrictive schools used their phones about 0.67 hours less during school time, but total use on weekdays and at weekends did not differ.
digital_resilience_e7.context: Cross-sectional study (SMART Schools), not randomised. However, more total phone and social media time was linked to poorer well-being, sleep and school performance – the authors conclude that school bans alone are not enough. Use to limit the expected health effect of phone-free schools to close to zero unless leisure use also decreases.

digital_resilience_e8.claim: Norwegian register study (477 lower secondary schools): phone bans reduced girls’ healthcare contacts for psychological symptoms and illnesses, reduced bullying for both sexes and improved girls’ grades and transition to academic upper secondary programmes – with the largest effect for girls from low socio-economic backgrounds.
digital_resilience_e8.context: Event study using administrative data 2010–2018. Working paper (NHH Discussion Paper 1/2024), not yet finally peer-reviewed at the time of checking; exact effect sizes could not be verified from the full text. Contrasts with Goodyear et al. 2025 (digital_resilience_e7) – the evidence is therefore mixed. In the model: a possible positive effect on girls’ mental health and equality, with an uncertainty interval that includes zero.

digital_resilience_e9.claim: According to UNESCO’s GEM Report, 79 education systems (40%) worldwide had bans on smartphones in school at the end of 2024, up from 60 (30%) at the end of 2023.
digital_resilience_e9.context: Based on UNESCO’s PEER database of laws and policies. Finland restricts phone use during lessons in basic education from 1 August 2025 (Finnish National Agency for Education, Utbildningsstyrelsen). Shows rapid policy diffusion – useful for arguing that ‘phone-free school’ has become the norm, not for effect size.

digital_resilience_e10.claim: Roughly one in ten in-store purchases in Sweden is made with cash (2024); in the euro area the share is about 50%.
digital_resilience_e10.context: The share fell sharply 2010–2020 and has since levelled off, with a small increase in 2023. Cash in circulation and cash withdrawals continue to decline. Model parameter for ‘payment redundancy’: low cash share = high vulnerability during digital outages unless offline solutions are in place.

digital_resilience_e11.claim: Since 1 July 2026, card payments with a physical card and PIN must work offline when buying essential goods (food, medicines, fuel) during disruptions to data communications for up to seven days. Sveriges Riksbank also recommends that households keep about SEK 1,000 in cash per adult.
digital_resilience_e11.context: Based on an agreement from October 2025 between Sveriges Riksbank, card issuers (including Handelsbanken, Nordea, SEB and Swedbank), Visa/Mastercard, acquirers and the retail sector (Ica, Coop, Axfood, Apoteket and others). Model parameter: number of days that basic retail keeps functioning during a telecoms/IT outage; the cash recommendation provides the household buffer.

digital_resilience_e12.claim: In 2026 the Riksdag decided (committee report 2025/26:FiU39, Government bill 2025/26:199) that grocery stores and pharmacies with staffed checkouts must, as a general rule, accept cash from 1 July 2026. The obligation applies to amounts up to 0.1 price base amounts and at most 25 coins per purchase.
digital_resilience_e12.context: Exceptions apply if staff safety cannot be maintained, if cash handling risks forcing the outlet to close, or if money laundering is suspected in the individual case. 0.1 price base amounts corresponds to about SEK 5,900 in 2026 (figure via a summary of the committee report). National constraint; the municipality can itself choose to accept cash in its own services.

digital_resilience_e13.claim: The brochure “Om krisen eller kriget kommer” (If Crisis or War Comes, 2024) urges everyone to be prepared at home for at least one week: at least three litres of water per person per day, a radio powered by batteries, solar cells or a crank, important phone numbers on paper, and cash in various denominations for at least one week. Sveriges Radio P4 is the emergency broadcast channel.
digital_resilience_e13.context: Published by the Swedish Civil Contingencies Agency (MSB) in 2024 (publ. no. MSB2398) and distributed to the country’s households in November 2024; since 2026 the agency has been called the Swedish Civil Defence and Resilience Agency (Myndigheten för civilt försvar, MCF) and the brochure is available at mcf.se. ‘Most of us will have to manage on our own for at least a week.’ Analogue reserves (paper, radio, cash) are thus official policy. Parameter: share of households prepared for one week.

digital_resilience_e14.claim: In 2025, 97% of Swedes (aged 16+) use the internet and 93% use it daily; 3% do not use the internet at all – almost exclusively people of retirement age. 95% use electronic ID.
digital_resilience_e14.context: National survey (Internetstiftelsen, the Swedish Internet Foundation). Practically everyone who lacks electronic ID is 65+.

digital_resilience_e15.claim: Almost a quarter of Swedes have refrained from booking a doctor’s appointment because healthcare e-services and apps are perceived as too difficult; more than one in ten feel that digital services make booking appointments harder.
digital_resilience_e15.context: Those most affected are the oldest, especially older women, people with disabilities and people born abroad – but also young adults.
