Shows that ‘digital first’ can lead to forgone care (health, equality). An exact percentage is not given in the summary; the value 25 is rounded up.

digital_resilience_e16.claim: Using a broader definition (rarely or never online), Internetstiftelsen (the Swedish Internet Foundation) estimated in 2018 that 1.1 million Swedes lived in digital exclusion, of whom 579,000 were over 76.
digital_resilience_e16.context: Older figure and broader definition than e14; corresponds to roughly one tenth of the population. Shows the range of 3–11% depending on definition. Verified via SVT’s reporting on Internetstiftelsen’s survey.

tech_ai_e1.claim: In the Swedish randomised MASAI trial (just over 105,900 women), AI-supported mammography screening found 29% more breast cancers (6.4 compared with 5.0 per 1,000 women screened) without significantly more false positives, and radiologists’ reading workload fell by 44%.
tech_ai_e1.context: Four screening units in south-western Sweden (Region Skåne) 2021–2022, AI system Transpara. The increase mainly concerned small lymph-node-negative invasive cancers and in situ cancer – some of this may be overdiagnosis. Model parameter for regional healthcare: early detection +, staffing need −44% in image reading.

tech_ai_e2.claim: MASAI’s primary outcome: interval cancer (cancer detected between screenings) was 1.55 per 1,000 in the AI group versus 1.76 in the control group (about 12% fewer), sensitivity was 80.5% versus 73.8%, and specificity was unchanged at 98.5%.
tech_ai_e2.context: Non-inferiority confirmed; the difference in interval cancer was not statistically significant (ratio 0.88, CI 0.65–1.18), but the AI group had fewer aggressive/large interval cancers (−27% aggressive subtypes according to Lund University). Published in The Lancet on 30 Jan 2026. Strengthens the case that AI screening is safe to introduce.

tech_ai_e3.claim: Experienced endoscopists who had become used to AI support found fewer adenomas when performing colonoscopy without AI: the adenoma detection rate fell from 28.4% to 22.4% (−6 percentage points, approx. −20% in relative terms).
tech_ai_e3.context: Observational study, four Polish centres, 19 endoscopists, 1,443 colonoscopies 2021–2022. The first study to suggest that regular AI use makes clinicians worse at tasks performed without AI. Model parameter for ‘deskilling’: if the AI system drops out (cyberattack, change of supplier), performance becomes worse than before AI.

tech_ai_e4.claim: Data centres used about 415 TWh of electricity in 2024, equivalent to about 1.5% of global electricity use; the USA accounted for 45%, China 25% and Europe 15%.
tech_ai_e4.context: The IEA’s best estimate. Data centre electricity use has grown by approx. 12%/year since 2017, four times faster than total electricity use. Emissions from data centre electricity are estimated at approx. 180 Mt CO2.

tech_ai_e5.claim: IEA base case: data centres’ electricity use more than doubles to about 945 TWh in 2030 and about 1,200 TWh in 2035 (range 700–1,700 TWh), with AI as the main driver; emissions rise from 180 to 300 Mt CO2.
tech_ai_e5.context: The range refers to 2035 across sensitivity scenarios. Relevant to Sweden as a host country for data centres (the AI Commission mentions, among other things, Microsoft’s SEK 33.7 billion investment in Swedish data centres).

tech_ai_e6.claim: AI-based fault location in power grids can shorten outage duration by 30–50%, and AI tools for grid operation can free up as much as 175 GW of transmission capacity globally without new power lines.
tech_ai_e6.context: The IEA’s compilation of applications. The 175 GW figure is global and refers in part to dynamic line rating. Model parameter for the local grid (e.g. The actual effect depends on metering data and grid structure.

tech_ai_e7.claim: The IEA estimates that broad application of existing AI solutions could reduce emissions by the equivalent of about 5% of energy-related emissions in 2035 – more than data centres’ own emissions, but not enough to solve the climate problem.
tech_ai_e7.context: Scenario calculation that assumes widespread adoption; rebound effects (e.g. cheaper transport leading to more travel) can eat up the gains. Use as a ceiling for AI’s climate benefit in the model, not as a certain effect.

tech_ai_e8.claim: According to Google’s own measurement, a median text prompt to Gemini (May 2025) used 0.24 Wh of electricity and 0.26 ml of water and produced 0.03 g CO2e; energy per prompt fell 33-fold in one year.
tech_ai_e8.context: The company’s self-reporting, not independently reviewed; refers to text prompts, not image/video or model training. Shows that individual use is small but that total volume and training drive demand (cf. tech_ai_e5). Model parameter: energy per AI interaction in municipal services.

tech_ai_e9.claim: AI-based flood forecasts achieve equal or better reliability for extreme flows with up to five days’ lead time than the global reference system GloFAS achieves in real time (zero days’ lead time), even in ungauged rivers; the system is used operationally in more than 80 countries.
tech_ai_e9.context: Peer-reviewed in Nature (Google Research et al.). Assumption in the model: earlier warning reduces damage; see also tech_ai_e10.

tech_ai_e10.claim: Only half of the world’s countries report adequate multi-hazard early warning systems; according to the WMO, early warning systems deliver an almost tenfold return on investment. The UN goal is for everyone to be protected by warning systems by the end of 2027.
tech_ai_e10.context: The WMO’s Early Warnings for All initiative. The return figure is a global summary; Swedish conditions (already well-developed warning systems: VMA (Important Public Announcements), SE-Alert) mean a lower marginal benefit. Used to justify AI-supported climate adaptation modelling.

tech_ai_e11.claim: In experiments with 5,734 participants, people preferred group statements written by an AI mediator (the ‘Habermas Machine’) to statements from human mediators – they were rated as more informative, clear and unbiased – and participants often moved towards a shared position. The result was replicated in a virtual citizens’ panel representative of the UK.
tech_ai_e11.context: Google DeepMind study in Science. Shows potential for AI-supported deliberation at scale (e.g. citizens’ assemblies, the comprehensive plan). Risks: the model’s values, manipulation, minority voices being smoothed out. The effect size on actual political participation is unknown.

tech_ai_e12.claim: The AI Commission’s roadmap contains 75 proposals estimated to cost SEK 16,712 million over ten years, of which SEK 11,507 million in the first five years. The Commission notes that smaller government agencies, small regions and municipalities ‘often have not even begun using AI’ and proposes a voluntary AI workshop for the public sector.
tech_ai_e12.context: SOU 2025:12, dated 2025-02-04 in the Riksdag’s document database. Approx. SEK 2.3 billion/year during the first five years. According to the Commission, the proposals do not restrict municipal self-government.

tech_ai_e13.claim: A rough estimate by the Agency for Digital Government (Digg) and McKinsey (2020) states that full use of today’s AI in public administration could yield gains of about SEK 140 billion per year, about 5–6% of public expenditure.
tech_ai_e13.context: The range gives % of public expenditure. Itself called a ‘rough estimate’ in SOU 2025:12; refers to full implementation and includes reduced incorrect payments. Should be seen as a theoretical ceiling – the benefit actually realised in a municipality is likely to be considerably lower (see tech_ai_e19).

tech_ai_e14.claim: Public administration spends around SEK 1.5 billion per year on interpreting services; AI-supported interpreting is realistically judged usable in 20–30% of interpreting situations, giving an annual savings potential of SEK 300–450 million. The Swedish National Courts Administration’s AI translation of legal text is estimated to cost 90% less than a translation agency and takes seconds instead of weeks.
tech_ai_e14.context: Range = savings potential in SEK billion/year. Example from SOU 2025:12. Risk: mistranslation in legal and medical contexts – a human interpreter is needed where mistakes have serious consequences.

tech_ai_e15.claim: The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) entered into force on 1 August 2024; the bans on unacceptable AI applications have applied since 2 February 2025, rules for general-purpose AI models since 2 August 2025, and the regulation applies in general from 2 August 2026.
tech_ai_e15.context: Prohibited: harmful manipulation and exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, individual crime-risk prediction, untargeted scraping of facial images, emotion recognition in workplaces and schools, biometric categorisation by sensitive characteristics, and real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement in publicly accessible spaces (with narrow exceptions). A ninth ban (non-consensual intimate material/CSAM) will be added in December 2026 via the AI omnibus. Sets a floor for municipal surveillance.

tech_ai_e16.claim: Through the AI omnibus (proposed 19 Nov 2025, political agreement 7 May 2026, in force 27 July 2026), the requirements for high-risk AI are postponed: for systems in areas such as biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment and migration they apply from 2 December 2027, and for AI in products (e.g. lifts, toys) from 2 August 2028.
tech_ai_e16.context: Relevant to municipal applications in schools, recruitment and energy/water (critical infrastructure). Until then, responsibility rests largely on the municipality’s own governance. Information from the European Commission’s website, October 2026; details may change.

tech_ai_e17.claim: Almost 40% of global employment and about 60% of jobs in advanced economies are exposed to AI; roughly half of the exposed jobs in advanced economies may benefit (productivity), while the rest risk lower labour demand, lower wages and fewer hires.
tech_ai_e17.context: IMF Staff Discussion Note (Cazzaniga et al. 2024), summarised by the head of the IMF. ‘Exposed’ does not mean replaced.

tech_ai_e18.claim: In 2025, 4 in 10 Swedes (aged 8+) use AI tools, as do 57% of children and young people aged 8–19. More than one in four people in employment use AI at work and one in three Swedes believe AI will cause high unemployment, but only 7% of those in employment worry about becoming unemployed themselves.
tech_ai_e18.context: An increase of 5 percentage points 2024–2025 (ages 18–84); men have overtaken women by 7 percentage points. One in five AI users has asked AI health questions (7% of the population). Starting value for AI adoption in the game; uneven adoption links to gender equality and the digital divide.

tech_ai_e19.claim: The City of Amsterdam has published around 80 algorithm descriptions in the Dutch public algorithm register, stating purpose, status (in use/in development/decommissioned) and impact assessments carried out (DPIA, ethical review).
tech_ai_e19.context: An example of a transparency instrument that a Swedish municipality could copy. The number changes over time. Helsinki has a similar AI register (not verified in this review).

tech_ai_e20.claim: Precision agriculture (variable-rate application of seed, fertiliser and pesticides, machine guidance, site-specific weed control) can reduce inputs and greenhouse gas emissions while maintaining or improving productivity and profitability.
tech_ai_e20.context: Review article (EU project). Exact percentage reductions vary greatly between technology, crop and farm and could not be verified in this review – model as an uncertain effect (assumption: −5 to −20% nitrogen and pesticide use with broad adoption, to be calibrated). Links to eutrophication of the Baltic Sea via nitrogen leaching.

resilience_e1.claim: The Swedish Civil Defence and Resilience Agency (MCF) recommends that households should be able to manage without help from society for at least one week (seven days), with water, food, heat and information.
resilience_e1.context: Official home preparedness recommendation from the Swedish Civil Defence and Resilience Agency (the Swedish Civil Contingencies Agency, MSB, was renamed MCF on 1 January 2026). Used as the target value for the indicator 'household self-sufficiency days'. The recommendation is normative – it says nothing about how many households actually meet it.

resilience_e2.claim: Households need at least three litres of water per person per day for home preparedness, plus food for at least seven days that can be stored at room temperature and prepared without electricity.
resilience_e2.context: From home preparedness information based on the brochure 'Om krisen eller kriget kommer' (If Crisis or War Comes), published on the website of the Swedish Civil Defence and Resilience Agency (MCF) (municipal version, Kinda Municipality). For a family of four over seven days, this equals at least 84 litres (own calculation: 4 × 3 × 7). Used as the design household stock in the model.

resilience_e3.claim: The new edition of the brochure 'Om krisen eller kriget kommer' (If Crisis or War Comes) was sent out in over 5 million copies to Sweden’s households on 18–29 November 2024, with a stronger focus on war preparedness than the 2018 version.
resilience_e3.context: Shows the state’s national information effort. Can be used as a reference for a municipal campaign (e.g.

resilience_e4.claim: The Swedish Food Agency’s planning levels for emergency water: 3–5 litres/person/day for the first few days (survival), 10–15 litres within 48–72 hours and for the following 10 days (drinking, cooking, basic hygiene), 50–100 litres during a prolonged water shortage in peacetime and 15 litres during a sustained crisis in wartime. Normal consumption is about 140 litres/person/day.
resilience_e4.context: The figures are reproduced in municipal emergency water plans (here Östhammar Municipality) with reference to the Swedish Food Agency’s calculations; normal consumption of 140 l is given with reference to Svenskt Vatten (the Swedish Water and Wastewater Association). The Swedish Food Agency’s own 'Guide för planering av nödvattenförsörjning' (Guide to planning emergency water supply, 2017) describes the methodology. In the model: the municipality’s emergency water capacity (m³/day) divided by the population gives litres/person/day, which is compared against the thresholds 5/10/15/50.

resilience_e5.claim: The starting point for total defence planning is to be able to cope, for at least three months, with a security policy crisis in Europe and Sweden’s neighbourhood involving serious disruption to the functioning of society, as well as war during part of that time.
resilience_e5.context: The Government’s guidelines for civil defence 2021–2025 (Government decision 2020-12-17, based on Government bill (prop.) 2020/21:30 Totalförsvaret 2021–2025). Used as the design endurance target for vital societal functions (healthcare, water, food, energy) in the municipality – separate from the households’ 7 days.

resilience_e6.claim: The Government is allocating SEK 575 million in the 2026 budget bill to emergency stockpiles, mainly grain and critical inputs for primary production; in September 2025 the Swedish Board of Agriculture was tasked with starting to purchase and store grain.
resilience_e6.context: Decision of 25 September 2025. Shows that food preparedness is being rebuilt nationally after the emergency stockpiles were dismantled following the Cold War. The municipality cannot build state stockpiles itself but can cooperate (e.g.

resilience_e7.claim: Sweden became NATO’s 32nd member on 7 March 2024. In 2023–2024, several critical undersea connections in the Baltic Sea were damaged: Balticconnector (gas, October 2023), two data cables Finland–Germany and Lithuania–Sweden (November 2024) and the Estlink 2 power cable (25 December 2024, suspected anchor dragging by the tanker Eagle S). In January 2025 NATO launched the surveillance operation Baltic Sentry.
resilience_e7.context: Background for the game’s 'threat level' and for justifying local redundancy in electricity, data and payments. No power outages occurred in Finland/Estonia in 2024 thanks to reserve capacity – an argument for redundancy rather than total self-sufficiency.

resilience_e14.claim: Seawater reverse osmosis (SWRO) typically uses 3.5–4.5 kWh of electricity per m³ of water produced; the range in the literature is 3–6.7 kWh/m³ depending on the raw water, quality requirements and plant efficiency.
resilience_e14.context: Applies to ocean seawater (~35 per mille salt). Used to link water security to the energy system: 3,000 m³/day × 4 kWh ≈ 12 MWh/day. Globally, in 2019, about 95 million m³ of desalinated water and 142 million m³ of brine were produced per day (Jones et al.

resilience_e19.claim: IPCC AR6: global mean sea level is projected to rise by 28–55 cm by 2100 under very low emissions (SSP1-1.9), 44–76 cm under intermediate emissions (SSP2-4.5) and 63–101 cm under very high emissions (SSP5-8.5), relative to 1995–2014.

resilience_e20.claim: Municipal crisis preparedness is governed by the Act (2006:544) on municipal and regional measures before and during extraordinary events in peacetime and periods of heightened alert (LEH): risk and vulnerability analyses, planning, geographical area responsibility, training and exercises, and reporting. A government inquiry was appointed in 2023 to replace LEH with more detailed regulation and to review funding.
resilience_e20.context: The framework for what the municipality must do (the floor) and what it can choose to do (the game’s policy choices). The inquiry’s terms of reference (30 March 2023, to report by 29 March 2024) state that the current regulation is not fit for purpose given the security situation.

resilience_e21.claim: Styrel is the national method for prioritising, in advance, vital electricity users if parts of the grid have to be disconnected during a power shortage. Municipalities, county administrative boards, grid companies and other actors set the priorities together; disconnections can be rotated so that no one is hit too hard.
resilience_e21.context: The priority classes range from 'critical to life and health (short term)' to 'other users'. Svenska kraftnät orders manual load shedding. In the model: the share of the municipality’s electricity demand that is 'priority load' determines how much local generation/storage is needed for island operation.

resilience_e23.claim: According to the Swedish Food Agency’s population survey (October 2025), 61% of Swedes (aged 16–84) have food at home that will last at least a week, but only 36% have enough to drink for a week. 78% have containers to store drinking water in and 63% have a way to cook food or boil water without electricity.
resilience_e23.context: Web panel conducted by Origo Group, n = 8,108, with about 1,000 interviews per NUTS2 area, weighted by area, gender and age. The shares are self-reported. Younger people (16–49) and tenants have smaller supplies than older people and homeowners. Only 48% correctly state that the authorities recommend a week’s supply of food and water. The values provide an empirical starting value for the indicator 'households with 7 days of home preparedness'. The share that manages both food and water is probably at most 36%.

biodiversity_baltic_e1.claim: The original planetary boundaries framework (2009) defined nine boundaries and assessed that three had already been transgressed: climate change, the rate of biodiversity loss and interference with the nitrogen cycle. The climate boundary was set at below 350 ppm carbon dioxide.
biodiversity_baltic_e1.context: Starting point for the game’s ecological ceiling. Published in Ecology and Society and in short form in Nature 461:472–475.

biodiversity_baltic_e2.claim: The third update (2023) quantified all nine boundaries for the first time and found that six of nine had been transgressed, with increasing pressure on all except the ozone layer.
biodiversity_baltic_e2.context: Richardson et al. 2023 in Science Advances 9(37). Summarised by the Stockholm Resilience Centre.

biodiversity_baltic_e3.claim: The Planetary Health Check 2025 (Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, PIK) assesses that seven of nine planetary boundaries have been transgressed; ocean acidification is the seventh boundary to be crossed.
biodiversity_baltic_e3.context: Annual report. Shows the trend of 3 → 6 → 7 transgressed boundaries over 2009–2025.

biodiversity_baltic_e4.claim: Over 96% of the Baltic Sea area is not in good status with regard to eutrophication, including the entire open sea and 86% of coastal waters (HELCOM assessment 2011–2016), despite a slight long-term improvement.
biodiversity_baltic_e4.context: From HELCOM’s updated Baltic Sea Action Plan (BSAP 2021, adopted in Lübeck on 20 October 2021, measures to be implemented by 2030). Status has recently deteriorated in four of 17 sub-basins.

biodiversity_baltic_e6.claim: Sweden’s net input ceiling (NIC) for inputs to the Baltic Proper is 30,690 tonnes of nitrogen and 318 tonnes of phosphorus per year. All measures required to meet the ceilings must be fully implemented by 2027.
biodiversity_baltic_e6.context: HELCOM BSAP 2021, tables 2a/2b. Provides a concrete 'budget' for the game’s nitrogen indicator.

biodiversity_baltic_e7.claim: Oxygen deficiency (hypoxia) in the Baltic Sea has increased tenfold over the past 115 years, mainly due to increased nutrient inputs from land; higher temperatures have worsened the situation over the past two decades.
biodiversity_baltic_e7.context: Reconstruction from oxygen and salinity profiles. The Baltic Sea is the world’s largest human-induced hypoxic area. Shows that warming and eutrophication interact – in the model, the climate scenario should make recovery harder.

biodiversity_baltic_e8.claim: Along the Swedish Baltic coast, a regime shift has taken place from dominance by large predatory fish (perch, pike) to three-spined stickleback. Fish surveys in 486 shallow bays along 1,200 km of coastline in 1979–2017 show that the shift began in the outer archipelago and has gradually spread towards the mainland coast; sticklebacks eat the predators’ fry, which reinforces the shift.
biodiversity_baltic_e8.context: Eklöf et al. 2020 (Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, SLU, and others). Seals and cormorants are discussed in the literature as contributing factors but are not included in this summary.

biodiversity_baltic_e9.claim: In July 2019 the EU introduced emergency measures (Implementing Regulation 2019/1248) banning targeted fishing for eastern Baltic cod in subdivisions 24–26, because the stock had unsustainably low biomass due to weak recruitment, environmental factors, high natural mortality and excessive fishing.
biodiversity_baltic_e9.context: Targeted cod fishing has since been closed in practice. The source is an environmental organisation’s summary of the regulation.

biodiversity_baltic_e10.claim: In the 2025 Red List (Rödlista 2025), 23,103 species in Sweden were assessed; 5,217 (nearly 23%) are red-listed and 2,373 (10%) are threatened. The number of red-listed species has increased by 10% since 2020 (from 4,746). The factors affecting the most red-listed species are overgrowth on land and a lack of continuity forest, followed by fishing (e.g. bottom trawling), land development, drainage of wetlands and climate change.
biodiversity_baltic_e10.context: Published on 24 March 2026 by the SLU Swedish Species Information Centre (SLU Artdatabanken; report 37). The increase is partly due to better knowledge. The otter and the white-tailed eagle left the list thanks to growing populations – measures work.

biodiversity_baltic_e11.claim: Constructed or restored wetlands remove a median of 93 g of nitrogen and 1.2 g of phosphorus per m² per year (equivalent to about 930 kg N and 12 kg P per hectare), with a median efficiency of 37% for nitrogen and 46% for phosphorus. Removal depends strongly on loading, temperature and wetland area.
biodiversity_baltic_e11.context: Systematic review (93 articles, 203 sites), partly funded by Mistra EviEM. The median is pushed up by heavily loaded wetlands (e.g. wastewater); agricultural wetlands with lower loading remove less per unit area – see the assumption in biodiversity_baltic_e18.

biodiversity_baltic_e12.claim: Non-legume catch crops (mainly ryegrass) undersown in spring cereals reduce nitrogen leaching by an average of 50% under Nordic conditions, at the cost of about 3% lower grain yield. Clover did not reduce the leaching risk but raised yields by 6%.
biodiversity_baltic_e12.context: Meta-analysis of 35 Nordic studies (Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Norway) on clay and coarse-textured soils, fertiliser rates of 50–160 kg N/ha and precipitation of 480–1,040 mm. The figures come from the authors’ 2016 EGU abstract of the article in Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment 203:93–101 (2015).

biodiversity_baltic_e13.claim: The environmental quality objective Thriving Wetlands (Myllrande våtmarker) will not be achieved (2025 assessment). Work on constructing, restoring and protecting wetlands is producing good results, but negative impacts continue from altered hydrology, climate change, invasive species and nitrogen deposition. Large areas of wetland have been drained since the early 19th century.
biodiversity_baltic_e13.context: Official follow-up of Sweden’s environmental objectives. Justifies an active wetland programme in the game.

biodiversity_baltic_e14.claim: In the plains of southern Sweden, an estimated 80–90% of the original wetlands have disappeared through drainage since the 19th century.
biodiversity_baltic_e14.context: The figure is often cited with reference to the Swedish Environmental Protection Agency, but has only been verified here in secondary sources (material from environmental organisations). Use it as an order of magnitude for restoration potential, not as an exact value.

biodiversity_baltic_e15.claim: The EU Nature Restoration Regulation (EU 2024/1991, in force 18 August 2024) requires restoration measures on at least 20% of the EU’s land and sea areas by 2030 and on all ecosystems in need of restoration by 2050. Among other things, it requires no net loss of urban green space and tree cover by 2030, that the decline of pollinators be reversed by 2030, and that at least 25,000 km of rivers be restored to free-flowing rivers. National restoration plans must be submitted by September 2026.
biodiversity_baltic_e15.context: In the game: a floor level that cannot be opted out of after 2030.

biodiversity_baltic_e20.claim: HELCOM’s updated Baltic Sea Action Plan (BSAP) was adopted on 20 October 2021 in Lübeck. It contains around 200 concrete actions in four segments (biodiversity, eutrophication, hazardous substances and litter, sea-based activities) to be implemented by 2030.
biodiversity_baltic_e20.context: HELCOM states 'about 200 concrete actions'. Other sources give exactly 199. The original plan from 2007 has helped reduce inputs of nutrients and hazardous substances, but the goal of a Baltic Sea unaffected by eutrophication was not achieved by 2021 (cf. biodiversity_baltic_e4). The year 2030 is thus a natural checkpoint in the game’s second decade.

governance_e1.claim: The Welsh Well-being of Future Generations Act sets out 7 statutory well-being goals and 5 mandatory ways of working (long term, prevention, integration, collaboration, involvement) for public bodies.
governance_e1.context: The goals: a prosperous, resilient, healthier and more equal Wales, cohesive communities, a vibrant culture and thriving Welsh language, and global responsibility. The Act originally covered 44 public bodies (local authorities, health boards, national parks, etc.); 8 bodies were added by regulations that came into force on 30 June 2024 (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/wsi/2024/775/made). The sustainable development principle in section 5 requires bodies to “balance short-term needs with the need to safeguard the ability to meet long-term needs”. Used in the game as a template for local well-being goals.

governance_e2.claim: The Future Generations Commissioner for Wales helped persuade the Welsh Government to halt the M4 relief road at Newport in June 2019, a road project estimated at about £1.4 billion.
governance_e2.context: In the report Transport Fit for Future Generations (Sept 2018) and at the public inquiry, Commissioner Sophie Howe argued that the project was contrary to the Act and proposed public transport and active travel at a fraction of the cost. First Minister Mark Drakeford took the decision; the official reasons were mainly cost and environmental impact, so the Commissioner’s causal role is a judgement. An example of how a future generations commissioner can influence major investments.

governance_e3.claim: Ten years after its adoption, the Act has gained greater prominence but is not driving the system-wide change that was intended, according to Wales’s public audit body (Audit Wales, April 2025).
governance_e3.context: The report “No time to lose” found good examples but also bodies that had given the Act no explicit consideration; health care lagged behind. Recommendations: reduce financial uncertainty, invest in prevention, review monitoring.

governance_e4.claim: The Finnish Parliament has had a Committee for the Future since 1993 (permanent since 2000) with 17 members, which conducts a dialogue with the Government on future issues and scrutinises the Government’s Report on the Future.
governance_e4.context: Set up in 1993 to scrutinise the Government’s first Report on the Future; a permanent committee since 2000. The 17 members and the move to permanent status in 2000 were confirmed via the Eduskunta website (search results) and a review by the United Nations University (Aceituno 2025), which counts at least 14 committees for the future or similar bodies worldwide. Research (Koskimaa & Raunio) describes the committee as unique but with limited direct influence on legislation. Local equivalent: a committee for the future in the municipal council.

governance_e5.claim: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy’s principle of the seventh generation means that decisions should take into account those who are not yet born but will inherit the world.
governance_e5.context: The Confederacy’s own website describes Seventh Generation as a core value: chiefs are to consider how today’s decisions affect their descendants, and nations are taught that they are “borrowing” the world from future generations. The principle is popularly attributed to the Great Law of Peace in varying wordings; the exact phrasings in circulation are often uncertain and should not be romanticised or taken out of their cultural context. Seven generations corresponds roughly to 150–200 years (our own calculation, 25–30 years per generation) – that is, longer than the game’s 100 years.

governance_e6.claim: None of just over 150 countries studied meets its inhabitants’ basic needs at a level of resource use that would be globally sustainable.
governance_e6.context: O’Neill et al. downscaled planetary boundaries to per capita level and compared them with social thresholds. Physical needs (nutrition, sanitation, electricity, eliminating extreme poverty) can probably be met for everyone within the boundaries, but more ambitious social goals currently require unsustainable resource use.

governance_e7.claim: The share of countries exceeding biophysical boundaries rose from 32–55% to 50–66% between 1992 and 2015, while social thresholds were achieved more slowly.
governance_e7.context: 11 social and 6 biophysical indicators for over 140 countries, 1992–2015. The share of countries reaching thresholds increased for five social indicators (e.g. life expectancy, education) but decreased for social support and equality. Business as usual to 2050 deepens the crisis. Used as a trend parameter: overshoot grows faster than social goal achievement.

governance_e8.claim: On 8 April 2020, Amsterdam adopted a circular strategy based on the Doughnut model, aiming to halve the use of new raw materials by 2030 and to be fully circular by 2050.
governance_e8.context: Kate Raworth and the Doughnut Economics Action Lab (DEAL) produced the “Amsterdam City Doughnut” as a basis. The city ran about 200 projects (sharing, repair, reuse). These are targets, not results achieved – the outcome for 2030 is not yet known.

governance_e9.claim: Tomelilla (about 7,000 inhabitants) is the first Swedish municipality to work with the Doughnut model: since 2021 in planning, monitoring and evaluation, and in 2024 the municipality published its first city portrait.
governance_e9.context: The Doughnut model has influenced investment decisions (renovating an existing building instead of building a new ice rink, according to The Guardian/DEAL 2025) and a new school project. Since May 2023, RISE has been running the project “The Doughnut Model in Municipal Sustainability Work” with Kalix, Tomelilla and Vadstena (https://www.ri.se/en/what-we-do/projects/the-doughnut-model-in-municipal-sustainability-work). Shows that even small Swedish municipalities can produce doughnut portraits.

governance_e10.claim: The Stockholm Resilience Centre’s “wedding cake” (Rockström & Sukhdev, 13 June 2016) shows the economy as embedded in society, which in turn is embedded in the biosphere.
governance_e10.context: Presented at the EAT Stockholm Food Forum 2016 as a way of moving beyond a sector-by-sector view of the Global Goals. The biosphere goals form the base. Useful for arranging the game’s indicators in three layers (biosphere – society – economy).

governance_e11.claim: To stay within 1.5 °C, lifestyle carbon footprints need to fall to 2.5 t CO2e per person per year by 2030 (current global average about 4.6 t).
governance_e11.context: Equity-based per capita targets: 2.5 t (2030), 1.4 t (2040), 0.7 t (2050). Refers to households’ lifestyle footprints (food, housing, transport, goods, leisure, services), and does not fully include public consumption and investment – compare with Sweden’s 7.6–8.3 t (governance_e13, e14) with caution. The report is grey literature from a think tank but builds on earlier peer-reviewed work (IGES/Aalto).

governance_e12.claim: The target level for 1.5-degree lifestyles in 2050 is 0.7 t CO2e per person per year (1.4 t in 2040).
governance_e12.context: Same source as governance_e11; the project website, which presents the 2025 update “A Climate for Sufficiency”, gives the same target levels. The Swedish Environmental Protection Agency gives a rough guideline of no more than 1 t CO2e per person per year globally by 2050.

governance_e13.claim: Sweden’s consumption-based greenhouse gas emissions were 80 million tonnes CO2e in 2023, an average of 7.6 tonnes per person, of which 64% occur abroad.
governance_e13.context: Includes household and public sector consumption as well as investment. A decrease from 110 Mt (2008) to 80 Mt (2023), −27%. Official statistics (Swedish Environmental Protection Agency/Statistics Sweden (SCB)). The page returned a 404 when checked on 2026-10-08 (probably moved); the figures were verified via the search engine’s excerpt of the page. Starting value for the game’s consumption indicator.

governance_e15.claim: Sweden is to reach net zero emissions by 2045 at the latest, which means that domestic emissions must be at least 85% lower than in 1990; in 2026 the Swedish Climate Policy Council judged the policies of the current term of office to have been inadequate.
governance_e15.context: The remaining 15% at most may be covered by supplementary measures (increased uptake in forests and land, bio-CCS, measures abroad). The Climate Act requires a climate report every year and an action plan every four years. The Climate Policy Council’s 2026 report (19 March): “the room for postponing decisions is exhausted” (https://www.klimatpolitiskaradet.se/rapport-2026/). According to media coverage of the Council’s 2025 report, emissions rose in 2024, partly as a result of the lowered fuel reduction obligation (not checked in the original report).

governance_e20.claim: Under the Planning and Building Act, every municipality must adopt a planning strategy each term of office (within 24 months of the election); otherwise the comprehensive plan ceases to be considered up to date.
governance_e20.context: The rule (in force since 2020) ties long-term comprehensive planning to the electoral cycle. It creates a recurring opportunity to revise a long-term vision – but also a risk that the vision is renegotiated every four years. The game’s decision rounds (decades) can mark two to three terms of office.

governance_e21.claim: In 2020, the Swedish Agency for Public Management (Statskontoret) found that the Government’s high ambitions for the 2030 Agenda had not yet had a noticeable impact on the sustainability work of municipalities, regions and government agencies, and that the level of ambition varied widely between different parts of the country.
governance_e21.context: Statskontoret 2020:15 (25 June 2020): most use the 2030 Agenda in some way, but there are few examples of far-reaching changes to their operations; small municipalities often lack capacity. In 2025 the Swedish National Audit Office (RiR 2025:22, “Statens arbete med Agenda 2030”, The central government’s work on the 2030 Agenda) concluded that central government’s work had not been effective and that the Government had not set out a clear direction (https://www.riksdagen.se/sv/dokument-och-lagar/dokument/betankande/riksrevisionens-rapport-om-statens-arbete-med_hd01fiu19/html/). Supports the claim that long-term vision-based governance is weak in Sweden – but it concerns the 2030 Agenda, not visions in general.

governance_e22.claim: Researchers on local government describe Swedish municipalities’ capacity for horizon scanning and strategic work as “rather weak”, and changes as usually small and incremental.
governance_e22.context: Kommuninvest’s research report (CERUM, CKS, KEFU, KFi) is based on interviews and documents in 11 municipalities and summarises the Natkom programme (2010–2016, 47 reports). Conclusion: a sustainable municipal future requires more inclusive, dialogue-based and experimental strategic work. Qualitative support for the view that municipalities lack long-term visions; not a representative survey.

governance_e23.claim: Sweden’s national work on the future has been temporary: the Commission on the Future of Sweden (Framtidskommissionen, 2011–2013) looked ahead to 2020 and 2050, and there was a minister for the future in 2014–2016, but there is no permanent institution for the future equivalent to those in Wales or Finland.
governance_e23.context: The Commission’s final report, Svenska framtidsutmaningar (Future Challenges for Sweden, Ds 2013:19), covered sustainable growth, demography, integration, democracy, gender equality and social cohesion. Kristina Persson was minister for strategy and future issues in 2014–2016, with three analysis groups (https://www.riksdagen.se/sv/dokument-och-lagar/dokument/svar-pa-skriftlig-fraga/funktionen-som-framtidsminister_h21238/). That no permanent institution exists is our conclusion from the review (low–medium confidence).

demography_e1.claim: Statistics Sweden (SCB) projects that Sweden’s population will be 11.8 million in 2070 (10.6 million in 2025 and 11.3 million in 2050).
demography_e1.context: Sveriges framtida befolkning 2026–2070 (The future population of Sweden 2026–2070, published 2026-04-16, Demografiska rapporter 2026:3). Growth in 2026–2030 is projected at only just over 5,000 per year, compared with 45,000 per year in 2021–2025. The share of foreign-born people rises from 21% (2025) to 25% (2070). Statistics Sweden (SCB) stresses that in the long term the projection is a calculation of what happens if current trends continue, not a forecast.

demography_e2.claim: In the Statistics Sweden (SCB) statistical database, the national projection extends to 2120: 12.96 million inhabitants in 2120, with more deaths than births in most years and net immigration of about 30,000 per year.
demography_e2.context: Table BefPrognosOversiktN (2026 projection): population 11.29 M (2050), 11.80 M (2070), 12.51 M (2100), 12.96 M (2120); about 114,000–124,000 births and about 119,000–131,000 deaths per year after 2060; net migration 29,500–36,000 per year. Retrieved via the Statistics Sweden (SCB) API on 2026-10-08. A mechanical extension with unchanged assumptions – highly uncertain, but the only official Swedish series that reaches the game’s final year. Shows that long-term population growth depends entirely on migration.

demography_e3.claim: Sweden’s total fertility rate was 1.43 children per woman in both 2024 and 2025 – the lowest level ever recorded (1.98 in 2010).
demography_e3.context: The series: 2.14 (1990), 1.50 (1999), 1.98 (2010), 1.67 (2020), 1.53 (2022), 1.45 (2023), 1.43 (2024), 1.43 (2025). In 2025, 97,500 children were born, the lowest number since 2002. The Government has appointed the inquiry “Framtid med barn” (A future with children) into the causes and consequences, due to report on 30 June 2028. Starting value for the game’s fertility parameter.

demography_e4.claim: Statistics Sweden (SCB) assumes that fertility among women born in Sweden will recover to a long-term level of 1.7 children per woman by the end of the projection period; in the long term, about 110,000 children are projected to be born per year.
demography_e4.context: The long-term assumptions are reviewed every three years (most recently in 2024, next in 2027). Statistics Sweden (SCB) points out that the assumption should be seen as an average future level, not the most likely level for any single year. If the recovery does not happen (remaining at ~1.4), the population will be smaller and older than in the main scenario – suitable as a scenario parameter for the game (1.4–1.8).

demography_e5.claim: Life expectancy was 85.5 years for women and 82.5 years for men in 2025 and is projected to rise to 89.7 and 87.5 years respectively by 2070.
demography_e5.context: Intermediate years: 86.3/83.5 (2035), 87.8/85.4 (2050). Life expectancy has risen by about 8 years (women) and 10 years (men) since 1970. The number of 100-year-olds is projected to rise from just under 3,000 (2025) to 13,500 (2070). Used for the game’s mortality parameter; in the model it is affected by health indicators.

demography_e6.claim: The share of the population aged 80 or over rises from just over 6% (2025) to 11.2% (2070), i.e. just over 1.3 million people.
demography_e6.context: According to the Statistics Sweden (SCB) database extension (our own calculation from table BefolkprognRevNb), the share aged 80+ will be 13.7% in 2100 and 13.6% in 2120. The share aged 20 or younger falls from just over 22% to 20%. Drives health and social care costs in the game.

demography_e7.claim: Sweden’s old-age dependency ratio (people aged 65+ per 100 people aged 20–64) rises from about 38 (2026) to about 52 (2070) and about 59 (2120).
demography_e7.context: Our own calculation from the Statistics Sweden (SCB) 2026 projection (table BefolkprognRevNb, retrieved via the API on 2026-10-08): 37.7 (2026), 45.5 (2050), 51.8 (2070), 56.5 (2100), 59.0 (2120). Total dependency ratio (0–19 + 65+ per 20–64): 0.77 → 0.89 → 0.98. Eurostat’s EUROPOP2023 gives 60.3 in 2100 (demography_e12) – consistent. A key parameter for the tax base versus welfare needs.

demography_e8.claim: Over the next ten years (2025–2035), Sweden is expected to have 165,000 fewer children of compulsory school age and 179,000 more people over 85.
demography_e8.context: At the same time: 30,000 more deaths than births, 200,000 more immigrants than emigrants, population +170,000. The number of people aged 85+ rises from 304,000 to 483,000 as the 1940s generation ages. Short-term planning parameter: schools risk overcapacity while elderly care needs to grow.

demography_e12.claim: Eurostat’s EUROPOP2023 (baseline) gives Sweden 12.1 million inhabitants in 2050, 12.9 million in 2070 and 13.3 million in 2100, with 14.0% aged 80+ and a median age of 48.2 years in 2100.
demography_e12.context: Higher than the Statistics Sweden (SCB) series (12.5 M in 2100) because the assumptions on migration and fertility differ. Old-age dependency ratio (65+/20–64): 36.5 (2025), 42.2 (2050), 60.3 (2100). Retrieved via the Eurostat API (tables proj_23np and proj_23ndbi) on 2026-10-08. Provides a reasonable upper range for the game’s scenarios.

demography_e14.claim: Swedish households are among the smallest in the EU (2.0 people on average compared with 2.3 in the EU in 2025), and young people leave the parental home early (at 23.1 years compared with 26.3 years in the EU in 2025).
demography_e14.context: Eurostat yth_demo_030 and ilc_lvph01 (retrieved via the API on 2026-10-08). The Swedish series has a break in 2021 (17.5 years in 2020, 22.0 years in 2021) and has risen since (21.6–21.9 years in 2022–2024, 23.1 years in 2025). Shows a strong norm of independent living – multigenerational living requires a cultural change, not just new housing.

demography_e15.claim: Caring for others – within and outside the family, e.g. grandparents looking after grandchildren – is associated with lower mortality for the person giving the care.
demography_e15.context: A prospective study of older people in Berlin (Berlin Aging Study). Observational data – an association, not proven causation (healthier older people may be able to look after children more often). We could only verify the title and metadata (Crossref), not the effect size in the abstract; therefore use only the direction, not a figure. Supports the idea that multigenerational solutions can benefit older people’s health.

demography_e16.claim: Stronger social relationships are associated with a 50% higher likelihood of survival over the follow-up period (OR 1.50; 95% CI 1.42–1.59) in a meta-analysis of 148 studies with 308,849 participants.
demography_e16.context: Holt-Lunstad et al. 2010: the effect is comparable to established risk factors such as smoking and alcohol. Relevant to demography because single-person households are numerous and the share of older people living alone is growing (demography_e13). See also the Community theme. Model parameter: link between social networks and mortality/health.

demography_e17.claim: The WHO guide to age-friendly cities (2007) provides a framework for making cities supportive and enabling for older people, so that their potential is put to good use.
demography_e17.context: The guide starts from the two megatrends of ageing and urbanisation and forms the basis of the WHO Global Network for Age-friendly Cities and Communities. We verified the guide and its purpose but not the list of domains in detail. Basis for levers on age-friendly urban planning.

quotes.text: the body must act in a manner which seeks to ensure that the needs of the present are met without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
quotes.who: Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015, section 5(1)

quotes.text: Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
quotes.who: World Commission on Environment and Development (Brundtland Commission), Our Common Future, 1987, ch. 2

quotes.text: Humanity’s 21st century challenge is to meet the needs of all within the means of the planet.
quotes.who: Kate Raworth, economist, originator of the Doughnut model (Doughnut Economics)

quotes.text: We propose a new approach to global sustainability in which we define planetary boundaries within which we expect that humanity can operate safely.
quotes.who: Johan Rockström et al., Planetary Boundaries: Exploring the Safe Operating Space for Humanity, Ecology and Society 2009

quotes.text: Nations are taught to respect the world in which they live as they are borrowing it from future generations.
quotes.who: Haudenosaunee Confederacy, on the value of the Seventh Generation

quotes.text: I raised serious concerns that the Black Route proposal was a short-term, 20th century solution that did not reflect or support the ambitions of the Well-being of Future Generations Act.
quotes.who: Sophie Howe, Future Generations Commissioner for Wales, on the decision to stop the M4 relief road, 5 June 2019

quotes.text: We cannot afford to design solutions that do not meet people’s needs, burden future generations with avoidable higher costs, or miss opportunities to deliver more with the same or less.
quotes.who: Adrian Crompton, Auditor General for Wales, 29 April 2025

quotes.text: The influence of social relationships on risk for mortality is comparable with well-established risk factors for mortality.
quotes.who: Julianne Holt-Lunstad, Timothy B. Smith, J. Bradley Layton, meta-analysis in PLoS Medicine 2010

quotes.text: If Sweden is attacked, we will never give up. All information suggesting that resistance is to cease is false.
quotes.who: Swedish Civil Contingencies Agency (MSB), the brochure Om krisen eller kriget kommer (If Crisis or War Comes) (MSB2398, November 2024; now the Swedish Civil Defence and Resilience Agency, MCF)
